"'''Bobby'''" '''Engram III''' (born January 7, 1973) is an American professional [[American football|football]] coach and former [[wide receiver]] who is the wide receivers coach for the [[Washington Commanders]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). Engram played [[college football]] for the [[Penn State Nittany Lions football|Penn State Nittany Lions]], earning the 1994 [[Fred Biletnikoff Award]], and was selected by the [[Chicago Bears]] in the second round of the [[1996 NFL draft]]. Engram also played for the [[Seattle Seahawks]] and [[Kansas City Chiefs]] before becoming a coach by the 2010s. ==Early life== Engram was born on January 7, 1973, in [[Camden, South Carolina]]. He attended [[Camden High School (South Carolina)|Camden High School]], where he was a three-time All-State selection at wide receiver. In 1991, Engram's father died in an automobile accident.{{cite news|last1=Parrillo|first1=Ray|title=For Now, Bobby Engram Is Professional In Demeanor Only|url=http://articles.philly.com/1995-09-03/sports/25718247_1_bobby-engram-penn-state-receiver|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141221224945/http://articles.philly.com/1995-09-03/sports/25718247_1_bobby-engram-penn-state-receiver|url-status=dead|archive-date=December 21, 2014|access-date=December 19, 2014|work=The Philadelphia Inquirer|date=September 3, 1995}} ==College career== Engram enrolled at [[Pennsylvania State University]] in 1991. In August 1992, he and fellow Nittany Lions receiver Rick Sayles were arrested and charged with felony counts of burglary, theft, and receiving stolen property when they entered an unlocked apartment to steal various electronics.{{cite news|last=Rudel|first=Neil|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/public-opinion-players-blow-a-golden-opp/181127394/|title=Players blow a golden opportunity|newspaper=[[Public Opinion (Chambersburg, Pennsylvania)|Public Opinion]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=August 27, 1992|access-date=September 15, 2025}} Both were suspended by the team while Engram received a semester-long suspension from the university, after which he dropped out of school.{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-star-ledger-paterno-faith-in-engram/181127535/|title=Paterno faith in Engram pays dividend|agency=[[Associated Press|AP]]|newspaper=[[The Star-Ledger]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=December 26, 1994|access-date=September 15, 2025}} Following a year in the [[Centre County, Pennsylvania|Centre County]]'s adult rehabilitation program, Engram re-enrolled and rejoined the team for the 1993 season.{{cite news|last=Wiseman|first=Steve|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-charlotte-observer-camdens-fallen-h/181127479/|title=Camden's fallen hero rises again|newspaper=[[The Charlotte Observer]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=December 29, 1993|access-date=September 15, 2025}} As a college junior, Engram was the go-to receiver on Penn State's undefeated 1994 team. He garnered [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] honors and won the inaugual [[Biletnikoff Award]], recognizing the season's outstanding college football receiver. Engram was the Nittany Lions' career receptions leader until 2008.{{cite web|url=http://www.centredaily.com/sports/story/966015.html |title=Butler works way into Penn State's record book |work=[[Centre Daily Times]] |last=Moody |first=Walt |date=November 16, 2008 |access-date=November 16, 2008 }}{{dead link|date=June 2016|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}} He is still the all-time leader in yards and touchdowns with 3,026 yards and 31 touchdowns.{{Cite web |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/penn-state/ |title=Penn State Nittany Lions Receiving |website=College Football at Sports-Reference.com |language=en |access-date=2019-05-31}} He also racked up 786 career punt return yards for the Nittany Lions, ranking him second in school history. He graduated in 1995 with a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree in exercise science. ==Professional career== {{NFL predraft | height ft = 5 | height in = 9 5/8 | weight = 187 | dash = | ten split = | twenty split = | shuttle = | cone drill = | vertical = | broad ft = | broad in = | bench = | arm span = 30 1/4 | hand span = 9 1/8 | wonderlic = | note = All values from [[NFL Combine]]{{Cite web |url=https://nflcombineresults.com/playerpage.php?f=Bobby&l=Engram&i=23229 |title=Bobby Engram, Combine Results, WR - Penn State |website=nflcombineresults.com |access-date=June 3, 2022}} }} ===Chicago Bears=== Engram was selected in the second round of the [[1996 NFL draft]], 52nd overall to the [[Chicago Bears]].{{Cite web |title=1996 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1996/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-30 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}} In his rookie season, he had 33 receptions for 389 yards and 6 touchdown catches. He also returned kicks. In 1999, he had his first 10-reception game in week 15 with 10 receptions for 94 yards and a touchdown, following this with a franchise-record 13 receptions 143 yards and two touchdowns.{{Cite web |title=Bobby Engram Career Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/E/EngrBo00/gamelog/ |access-date=2025-09-22 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}[https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/E/EngrBo00/gamelog/ Bobby Engram game log] The following season, he had just 16 receptions in three games before injury ended his 5 seasons with the Bears. ===Seattle Seahawks=== Engram signed with the [[Seattle Seahawks]] before the 2001 season. He would spend 8 seasons with the Seahawks and reached the 1,000-yard receiving threshold in 2007 (94 catches, 1,147 yards), which was the only 1,000-yard season of his career. Despite being a [[Starting lineup|starter]] in only 67 of the 109 games he played with Seattle, Engram ranks fifth in franchise history in receptions (399) and fourth in receiving yards (4,859).{{cite web | url = http://www.seahawks.com/news/articles/article-1/Quite-the-catch/26646738-f648-4973-9be6-5634424e6976 | title = Quite the catch | publisher = Seattle Seahawks | first = Clare | last = Farnsworth | date = May 17, 2011 | access-date = January 15, 2012 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20120612035807/http://www.seahawks.com/news/articles/article-1/Quite-the-catch/26646738-f648-4973-9be6-5634424e6976 | archive-date = June 12, 2012 | url-status = dead | df = mdy-all }} His 94 receptions in [[2007 Seattle Seahawks season|2007]] was a Seahawks single-season record (since surpassed by [[Tyler Lockett]]), and he led the team in catches during the team's [[Super Bowl XL]] season in [[2005 Seattle Seahawks season|2005]] with 67. Engram was named to the Seahawks' 35th Anniversary Team in 2011.{{cite web | url = http://blog.seahawks.com/2011/05/17/engram-humbled-by-selection | title = Engram 'humbled' by selection | publisher = Seattle Seahawks | first = Clare | last = Farnsworth | date = May 17, 2011 | access-date = January 15, 2012 | archive-date = May 21, 2011 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20110521041021/http://blog.seahawks.com/2011/05/17/engram-humbled-by-selection/ | url-status = dead }} ===Kansas City Chiefs=== Engram joined the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] in 2009, but only played in 5 games for the team. ===Cleveland Browns=== Engram signed with the [[Cleveland Browns]] in the 2010 preseason, but failed to make the roster and was released before the regular season began. ===Retirement=== On January 28, 2011, Engram announced his retirement from playing.{{cite web | url = https://www.espn.com/blog/nflnation/post/_/id/36655/welcoming-bobby-engram-back-to-west | title = Welcoming Bobby Engram back to West | work = [[ESPN.com]] | first = Mike | last = Sando | date = January 28, 2011}} ==NFL career statistics== {| class="wikitable" ! colspan="2"| Legend |- | '''Bold''' | Career high |} ===Regular season=== {| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center;" |- ! rowspan="2"| Year ! rowspan="2"| Team ! colspan="2"| Games ! colspan="5"| Receiving ! colspan="5"| Rushing |- ! '''Bobby Lee Bell Sr.''' (born June 17, 1940) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] and [[defensive end]] for the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] of the [[American Football League]] (AFL) and the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Minnesota Golden Gophers football|Minnesota Golden Gophers]]. Bell is a member of the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]], [[College Football Hall of Fame]], [[NFL 100th Anniversary All-Time Team]], and played on the Chiefs' team that won [[Super Bowl IV]]. [[Paul Zimmerman (sportswriter)|Paul Zimmerman]] described him as the first, and prototype, size and speed linebacker.

==Early life==
Bell was born on June 17, 1940, in the [[Racial segregation|segregated]] city of [[Shelby, North Carolina]].<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Star |first=Vahe Gregorian The Kansas City |date=2021-09-10 |title=COLUMN {{!}} Chiefs great Bobby Bell a monument to change |url=https://themercury.com/townnews/building_industry/column-chiefs-great-bobby-bell-a-monument-to-change/article_71376e9d-7917-5d98-ac9c-80fca4bcdf3a.html |access-date=2024-11-01 |website=The Mercury |language=en}}</ref> When he was six years old, he was asleep in the family home, owned by the [[Textile manufacturing|textile mill]] employing his father, when it caught fire. His mother, Zannie Lee Bell, broke free from those trying to restrain her from going into the collapsing building, where she crawled on the floor to his bedroom and pulled him out to safety. Bell had a scar on his head from this incident the rest of his life. Bell's father, Pink Lee Bell, worked in various jobs at the town's textile mill.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3">{{Cite news |last=Pogash |first=Carol |date=December 19, 2014 |title=A Champion at 20. A Graduate at 74 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2014/12/20/sports/football/bobby-lee-bell-an-nfl-star-honors-his-father-by-accomplishing-one-more-goal.html |work=The New York Times}}</ref> 

Bell excelled in several sports at Cleveland High School in Shelby, where he was coached by John Winston in football.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Bobby Bell |publisher=Pro Football Hall of Fame |url=https://www.profootballhof.com/players/bobby-bell/ |access-date=2024-11-01 |language=en}}</ref> He was scouted by the [[Chicago White Sox]] for [[baseball]] at 16 years old, but his father wanted him to finish school. In his first two years of high school, he played [[six-man football]], playing under center at the position of [[Halfback (American football)|halfback]]. During his junior year, his school converted to playing as an [[American football|11-man football team]], where Bell played [[quarterback]]. He would receive All-State honors in football at both halfback and quarterback.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":0" /><ref name=":5">{{Cite web |title=Gold Jacket Spotlight: Bobby Bell Could Play Any Position |publisher=Pro Football Hall of Fame |url=https://www.profootballhof.com/news/2021/05/gold-jacket-spotlight-bobby-bell-could-play-any-position/ |access-date=2024-11-01 |language=en}}</ref>

==College career==
Coach [[Jim Tatum]] of the [[University of North Carolina]] was interested in Bell to play football, but the school was segregated. Tatum contacted coach [[Murray Warmath]] at the [[University of Minnesota]], where Warmath had been recruiting black players. Tatum recommended Bell, and Bell went to Minnesota. At Minnesota, it was the first time he shared a classroom or dining table with whites. Bell was originally a quarterback, but Warmath switched him to the defensive line. Bell would also play offensive tackle and center.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":0" /> Warmath said of Bell, "'He would have been a standout at any position; he was of maximum value to us at tackle.'"<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Bobby Bell |publisher=College Football Hall of Fame |url=https://www.cfbhall.com/inductees/bobby-bell-1991#:~:text=Robert%20Lee%20Bell%2C%20Jr.%20was%20a%20Tackle%20for,into%20College%20Football%20Hall%20of%20Fame%20in%201991}}</ref>

The [[Minnesota Golden Gophers football|Gophers]] with Bell had a record of 22-6-1, were the 1960 [[NCAA Division I-A national football championship|National Champions]], played in the [[1961 Rose Bowl]], and won the [[1962 Rose Bowl]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> 

He was a two-time first-team [[All-American]] (1961 and 1962) and the winner of the 1962 [[Outland Trophy]], which is given to the nation's most outstanding interior lineman. In 1962, he was also named Lineman of the Year by the United Press and the Columbus Touchdown Club as well as Player of the Year by Coach & Athlete Magazine. He also finished third in [[Heisman Trophy]] voting.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" />

Bell played superbly on defense in the 1963 [[Chicago Charities College All-Star Game|Chicago College All Star Game]], where the college players upset the defending NFL champion [[1963 Green Bay Packers season|Green Bay Packers]]. Packers legendary head coach [[Vince Lombardi]] called this his most embarrassing loss as a coach.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Blanchard |first=Ken |date=August 3, 1963 |title=Battin' the Breeze With Ken Blanchard, Otto Had A Great Bunch |work=The La Crosse Tribune (La Crosse, Wisconsin) |pages=4}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Hendricks |first=Martin |title=50 years ago: Haunted by earlier loss, Lombardi's Packers roll past College All-Stars, 27-0 |url=https://www.packersnews.com/story/sports/nfl/packers/2017/08/04/years-ago-haunted-earlier-loss-lombardis-packers-roll-past-college-stars/104240084/ |access-date=2025-09-06 |website=Packers News |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Vince Lombardi {{!}} Pro Football Hall of Fame {{!}} Pro Football Hall of Fame |url=https://www.profootballhof.com/players/vince-lombardi |access-date=2025-09-09 |website=pfhof |language=en}}</ref> 

Bell joined the [[Alpha Phi Alpha]] fraternity, via the Mu Chapter, while at the University of Minnesota.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Craige |first=Brent |date=2022-04-20 |title=Pro Football Hall Of Famer Bobby Bell Is A Member Of Alpha Phi Alpha |url=https://www.watchtheyard.com/alphas/pro-football-hall-of-famer-bobby-bell-is-a-member-of-alpha-phi-alpha/ |access-date=2024-11-01 |website=Watch The Yard |language=en-US}}</ref> 

==Professional football career==
Bell was selected by the Minnesota Vikings of the NFL in the second round (16th overall),<ref name=":5" /> and in the seventh round of the AFL draft by the Kansas City Chiefs. He surprisingly chose to join the Chiefs, where he would go on to play for 12 years, first in the [[American Football League]] from [[1963 American Football League season|1963]] through [[1969 American Football League season|1969]], and then in the NFL from [[1970 NFL season|1970]] through [[1974 NFL season|1974]]. He met with Chiefs owner [[Lamar Hunt]] over ice cream on Minnesota's campus, and they agreed to a no-cut guaranteed contract, something the Vikings would not do; in addition to agreeing to a longer term of years than the Vikings offered.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":4" /> 

In 1964, Bell was All-AFL as a defensive end,<ref>{{Cite web |title=1964 AFL All-Pros |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1964_AFL/allpro.htm |access-date=2026-01-19 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> but in 1965, future [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] coach [[Hank Stram]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=Hank Stram {{!}} Pro Football Hall of Fame |url=https://www.profootballhof.com/players/hank-stram |access-date=2025-09-09 |website=pfhof |language=en}}</ref> moved Bell to [[Linebacker|outside linebacker]]. Stram moved Bell to outside linebacker for his speed to combat the [[Oakland Raiders]]' use of running back [[Clem Daniels]] as a pass receiver out of the backfield.<ref name=":9" /> Bell was then selected first-team All-AFL or All-NFL as a linebacker every year from 1965 to 1971 by the [[Associated Press]], [[United Press International]], the [[Newspaper Enterprise Association]] and/or [[The Sporting News|''The Sporting News'']].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1965 AFL and NFL Awards |url=https://www.profootballarchives.com/1965awards.html |access-date=2026-01-19 |website=www.profootballarchives.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=1965 AFL All-Pros |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1965_AFL/allpro.htm |access-date=2026-01-19 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=1966 AFL and NFL Awards |url=https://www.profootballarchives.com/1966awards.html |access-date=2026-01-19 |website=www.profootballarchives.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=1966 AFL All-Pros |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1966_AFL/allpro.htm |access-date=2026-01-19 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=1967 AFL All-Pros |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1967_AFL/allpro.htm |access-date=2026-01-19 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=1968 AFL All-Pros |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1968_AFL/allpro.htm |access-date=2026-01-19 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=1969 AFL All-Pros |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1969_AFL/allpro.htm |access-date=2026-01-19 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=1970 NFL All-Pros |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1970/allpro.htm |access-date=2026-01-19 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=1971 NFL All-Pros |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1971/allpro.htm |access-date=2026-01-19 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> Bell was an [[American Football League All-Star games|AFL All-Star]] for six consecutive years, [[1964 AFL season|1964]] through [[1969 AFL season|1969]], and then an NFL [[Pro Bowl]]er for four straight years ([[1970 Pro Bowl|1970]], [[1971 Pro Bowl|1971]], [[1972 Pro Bowl|1972]], [[1973 Pro Bowl|1973]]).<ref name=":0" /> He was AFL Defensive Player of the Year in 1969.<ref name=":6">{{Cite web |title=Bobby Bell – Missouri Sports Hall of Fame |url=https://mosportshalloffame.com/inductees/bobby-bell/ |access-date=2024-11-01 |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":4" /> Bell never missed a regular season game, playing in 168 during his professional career.<ref name=":5" />

Bell was one of the first black outside linebackers in professional football.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":4">{{Cite news |last=Taylor |first=Nate |date=July 21, 2021 |title=NFL 100: At No. 74, Bobby Bell blended rare athleticism, smarts as Chiefs' superstar linebacker |url=https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/2710350/2021/07/21/nfl-100-at-no-74-bobby-bell-blended-rare-athleticism-smarts-as-chiefs-superstar-linebacker/ |access-date=2024-11-01 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> The 1965 AFL All-Star Game was moved from New Orleans to Houston because the black and white players would not have been allowed to dine together in the same New Orleans restaurant.<ref name=":3" />  

He was on two AFL Championship teams (1966 and 1969) and a World Championship team, losing [[Super Bowl I]] and winning Super Bowl IV.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Kansas City Chiefs Team Records, Leaders, and League Ranks |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/kan/index.htm |access-date=2024-11-01 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He was named to the first team [[American Football League All-Time Team|All-Time All-AFL Team]] in 1970, along with teammates [[Jerry Mays (defensive lineman)|Jerry Mays]], future Hall of Famer [[Johnny Robinson (safety)|Johnny Robinson]],<ref name=":7">{{Cite web |title=Johnny Robinson {{!}} Pro Football Hall of Fame |url=https://www.profootballhof.com/players/johnny-robinson |access-date=2025-09-09 |website=pfhof |language=en}}</ref> [[Fred Arbanas]], [[Ed Budde]], [[Jim Tyrer]], [[Paul Lowe]] and [[Jerrel Wilson]] on the first team, and future Hall of Famers [[Buck Buchanan]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=Junious (Buck) Buchanan {{!}} Pro Football Hall of Fame |url=https://www.profootballhof.com/players/junious-buck-buchanan |access-date=2025-09-09 |website=pfhof |language=en}}</ref> and [[Len Dawson]]<ref name=":8">{{Cite web |title=Len Dawson {{!}} Pro Football Hall of Fame |url=https://www.profootballhof.com/players/len-dawson |access-date=2025-09-09 |website=pfhof |language=en}}</ref> on the second team.<ref>{{Cite web |title=American Football League All-time Team |url=http://remembertheafl.com/AFLAllTimeTeam.htm |access-date=2024-11-01 |website=remembertheafl.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Tobias |first=Todd |title=>The AFL All-Time Second Team |url=https://talesfromtheamericanfootballleague.com/the-afl-all-time-second-team/ |access-date=2024-11-01 |website=Tales from the AFL |language=en-US}}</ref>  

A total of six defensive players on the Chiefs Super Bowl IV championship team were selected to the Pro Football Hall of Fame (Bell, Buchanan, [[Curley Culp|Curly Culp]], [[Willie Lanier]], [[Emmitt Thomas]] and Johnny Robinson).<ref name=":32">{{Cite web |last=Verderame |first=Matt |date=2015-02-09 |title=The '69 Chiefs: A defense for the ages |url=https://www.arrowheadpride.com/2015/2/9/7871727/1969-kansas-city-chiefs-defense-super-bowl-history |access-date=2024-11-01 |website=Arrowhead Pride |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":7" /> Quarterback Len Dawson and kicker Jan Stenerud from that team are also in the Hall of Fame.<ref name=":8" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Jan Stenerud |publisher=Pro Football Hall of Fame |url=https://www.profootballhof.com/players/jan-stenerud/ |access-date=2024-11-01 |language=en}}</ref> He played alongside Hall of Fame middle linebacker Willie Lanier,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Doerschuk |first=Steve |title=Nitschke and Robinson were close friends, teammates |url=https://www.cantonrep.com/story/sports/pro/pro-football-hof/2013/07/31/nitschke-robinson-were-close-friends/42239159007/ |access-date=2024-11-01 |website=Canton Repository |language=en-US}}</ref> and was part of one of the all-time linebacker trios with Lanier and [[Jim Lynch]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Tobias |first=Todd |title=Top 10 Linebacking Corps: #4 Hank Stram's Chiefs |url=https://talesfromtheamericanfootballleague.com/top-10-linebacking-corps-4-hank-strams-chiefs/ |access-date=2024-11-02 |website=Tales from the AFL |language=en-US}}</ref> 

One of Bell's finest moments came in the [[AFL playoffs, 1969|1969 AFL divisional playoff]] game against the [[New York Jets]]. In a critical [[Goal line (American football)|goal line]] stand, his key coverage on Jets [[running back]] [[Matt Snell]] stopped the drive and forced New York to kick a [[field goal]]. Jets quarterback [[Joe Namath]] was stunned Bell was in coverage and said it would have otherwise been a touchdown and Jets victory.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":4" /> The 13–6 victory over the Jets propelled [[Kansas City Chiefs|Kansas City]] to its first [[Super Bowl]] triumph. During a regular-season game against Denver (11/27), the Broncos, trailing 24–17 late in the game, attempted an onside kick that was recovered by Bell, who promptly returned that kick for a 53-yard touchdown.<ref name="Chiefs History">[http://www.kcchiefs.com/history/60s/ Chiefs History: 1960's] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070124191953/http://www.kcchiefs.com/history/60s/ |date=January 24, 2007 }} ''KCChiefs.com'', retrieved January 1, 2007.</ref>

He was also a [[Blitz (American football)|blitzer]] from the linebacker position.<ref name=":4" /> Bell played left side linebacker in Stram's "stack defense".<ref name=":5" /> Chiefs records show Bell had 40 career [[quarterback sack]]s<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bobby Bell Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/B/BellBo00.htm |access-date=2024-11-01 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":0" /> and he might have had more if he had played right linebacker, not the left linebacker. In that era, more often than not the right-side linebacker got the call to "dog" or blitz since more often than not the [[tight end]] would be lined up right, on the defense's left. {{citation needed|date=November 2024}} 

Bell scored nine [[touchdown]]s in his career: six off [[interception]]s (tied for most in NFL history for a linebacker with [[Derrick Brooks]]),<ref>{{cite web|last=Mayer|first=Larry|url=http://www.chicagobears.com/news/article-1/Briggs-adjusting-to-new-role-as-defensive-play-caller/18851b86-4124-459f-bede-5b2b9a54ca09|title=Briggs adjusting to new role as defensive play-caller|publisher=[[Chicago Bears]]|date=July 26, 2013|access-date=July 26, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130730074403/http://www.chicagobears.com/news/article-1/Briggs-adjusting-to-new-role-as-defensive-play-caller/18851b86-4124-459f-bede-5b2b9a54ca09|archive-date=July 30, 2013|url-status=dead}}</ref> two more touchdowns off [[fumble]] recoveries, and one off an [[onside kick]]off return.<ref name=":0" /> In his Hall of Fame induction speech for Bell, Stram described Bell as the only player who could play any position on a winning football team.<ref name=":0" /> Stram said that, "He could play all 22 positions on the field, and play them well."<ref>{{Cite web |title=Kansas City Chiefs: Top 10 NFL Draft Picks of All-Time |url=https://www.foxsports.com/stories/nfl/kansas-city-chiefs-top-10-nfl-draft-picks-of-all-time |access-date=2024-11-01 |work=Fox Sports |language=en-US}}</ref> In addition to all that, Bell had been a center in college and played long snapper for the Chiefs.<ref name=":4" /> He was regarded as one of the greatest long snapper centers for field goals and points-after-touchdowns in NCAA and AFL/NFL history.{{citation needed|date=March 2026}} Kansas City Chiefs' punter [[Jerrel Wilson]], who was selected by the Pro Football Hall of Fame as the punter on the [[American Football League All-Time Team|AFL's All-Time Team]] attributed much of his punting success to Bell's superb long snapping. Wilson called Bell the greatest long snapper in football.<ref name=":14">{{Cite news |last=Covitz|first=Randy|date=March 6, 1988|title=Just for kicks, Chiefs decide to add Jerrel Wilson to Hall|work=The Kansas City Star|pages=2, Sports}}</ref><ref name=":10">{{Cite web |title=AFL Hall of Fame All-Decade Teams - 1960s|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/awards/|access-date=2026-03-31|website=Pro-Football-Reference.com|language=en}}</ref>

== Legacy and honors ==
Bell was noted for his one-of-a-kind athleticism. At 6 ft 4 in (1.93 m) and 220 (99.8 kg) or 230 (104.3 kg) pounds, with a 28-inch (71.1 cm) waist and pyramid-like build, he was also reported to have run a 4.4 or 4.5 [[40-yard dash]].<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":4" /> Some consider Bell "the greatest all-around athlete to have played football".<ref name=":5" /> Bell was possibly the most physically gifted linebacker in professional football history, for his speed at such a size made him ideal at outside linebacker.{{citation needed|date=February 2020}} He was considered one of the finest open-field tacklers in [[professional football (gridiron)|professional football]] history.<ref name=":0" /> He has been called the first great "size and speed" linebacker and the "prototype speed linebacker".<ref name=":9">{{Cite magazine |last=Zimmerman |first=Paul |date=September 4, 1985 |title=The Best Athletes on the Field |url=https://vault.si.com/vault/1985/09/04/the-best-athletes-on-the-field |magazine=Sports Illustrated}}</ref>

In 2019, Bell was selected to the [[NFL 100th Anniversary All-Time Team]], which also included teammates [[Buck Buchanan]], [[Willie Lanier]] (who would become a lifelong friend<ref name=":4" />),  and [[Jan Stenerud]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=NFL 100 |url=https://www.nfl.com/100/all-time-team/roster |access-date=2024-11-01 |publisher=NFL |language=en-US}}</ref> In 1999, he was ranked number 66 on ''[[The Sporting News]]''' list of the 100 Greatest Football Players, one above teammate Buck Buchanan.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Sporting News 100 Greatest Players of All-Time (1999) |url=https://futurefootballlegends.com/Sporting_News_100/ |access-date=2024-11-01 |website=Future Football Legends}}</ref> He was number 74 on ''[[the Athletic]]''{{'}}s 2021 list of the best 100 football players of all time.<ref name=":4" />

Bell was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 1983.<ref name=":0" /> In 1970, he was selected as first-team on the AFL's All-Time Team.<ref name=":10" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=American Football League All-time Team |url=http://www.remembertheafl.com/AFLAllTimeTeam.htm |access-date=2025-09-14 |website=www.remembertheafl.com}}</ref> In 1991, he was inducted into the College Football Hall of Fame.<ref name=":1" /> In 1980, he was inducted into the Kansas City Chiefs Hall of Fame,<ref name=":0" /> the first Chief to receive that honor.<ref name=":2" /> The Chiefs retired his uniform number 78.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Goldsmith |first=Reid |date=2020-07-28 |title=Kansas City Chiefs Retired Numbers |url=https://clutchpoints.com/kansas-city-chiefs-retired-numbers |access-date=2024-11-01 |website=ClutchPoints {{!}} NFL News |language=en}}</ref> He was inducted into the Missouri Sports Hall of Fame in 1995, and named one of its Legends in 2006.<ref name=":6" />

On August 22, 2016, The Tournament of Roses announced Bobby Bell, [[Ricky Ervins]], [[Tommy Prothro]], and [[Art Spander]] would be inducted into the Rose Bowl Hall of Fame as the Class of 2016.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bobby Bell (2016) - Rose Bowl Hall of Fame |url=https://rosebowlgame.com/honors/rose-bowl-hall-of-fame/bobby-bell/118 |access-date=2024-11-01 |publisher=Tournament of Roses - Rose Bowl Game |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Rose Bowl Hall of Fame |url=https://rosebowlgame.com/honors/rose-bowl-hall-of-fame?type=class_induction |access-date=2024-11-01 |publisher=Tournament of Roses - Rose Bowl Game |language=en}}</ref> The Rose Bowl Hall of Fame Induction Ceremony then took place on January 1, 2017, outside the Rose Bowl Stadium, one day before the kickoff of the 103rd Rose Bowl game on Monday, January 2, 2017.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bobby Bell Will Be Inducted Into Rose Bowl Hall of Fame This Weekend |url=https://www.chiefs.com/news/bobby-bell-will-be-inducted-into-rose-bowl-hall-of-fame-this-weekend-18360524 |access-date=2024-11-01 |publisher=Kansas City Chiefs |language=en-US}}</ref>

The Bobby Bell Award is presented annually as part of the [[Simone Awards|Thomas A. Simone Annual Memorial Football Awards]] to a high school player in the greater Kansas City, Missouri area for outstanding small class defensive lineman/linebacker.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Simone Memorial Awards |url=https://www.neccoraiders73.com/simoneawards |access-date=2024-12-13 |website=Necco Raiders Youth Football & Cheerleading |language=en-us}}</ref>

While at the University of Minnesota, Bell joined Minnesota's basketball team as a walk-on, becoming its first black player.<ref name=":3" /> 

== Personal life ==
After his success at the University of Minnesota, Bell was offered the key to the city of Shelby in 1962. Instead, he asked if he could walk into the front door of the ice cream parlor across the street to get an ice-cream cone. Shelby was still a segregated city, and he was refused.<ref name=":2" /> There is now an historical marker for Bell in Shelby.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bobby Bell Historical Marker |url=https://www.hmdb.org/m.asp?m=199338 |access-date=2024-11-01 |website=hmdb.org |language=en}}</ref> On August 28, 2021, there was a Bobby Bell Day in Shelby, that included unveiling a sign for Bobby Bell Boulevard, dedicating a muraled wall of a building with his images, and renaming the City Pavilion the Bobby Bell Pavilion.<ref name=":2" />

After his retirement, he opened ''Bobby Bell's Bar-b-que'' in [[Kansas City, Missouri]], which he operated for nearly thirty years.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":4" /> He was a motivational speaker for many years.<ref name=":4" />

Bell left the University of Minnesota 13 credits short of a degree, to play for the Chiefs. At the age of 74, he completed his college degree at Minnesota by finishing the three remaining courses he required. He graduated on May 14, 2015, some 50 years after leaving college to play professional football. He did it to honor his father, who believed that blacks could compete equally with whites in sports and education if given a chance. Before going to Minnesota, Pink Lee Bell had given his son a gold watch, so he would never be late for class.<ref name=":3" /> Bell wore that watch 55 years later during his graduation ceremony.<ref name=":4" />

'''Bobby Joseph Hebert Jr.''' (surname pronounced {{respell|AY|bair}} {{IPAc-en|ˈ|eɪ|b|ɛər}}; born August 19, 1960) is an American [[sportscaster]] and former professional [[American football|football]] [[quarterback]]. He played in the [[United States Football League]] (USFL) and [[National Football League]] (NFL) from 1983 to 1996 for the [[Michigan Panthers]], [[Oakland Invaders]], [[New Orleans Saints]], and [[Atlanta Falcons]]. Nicknamed "'''the Cajun Cannon'''", Hebert led the Panthers to the USFL championship in the league's inaugural season. Later he helped bring the Saints their first winning season and playoff appearance in franchise history. Hebert was inducted to the New Orleans Saints Hall of Fame in 1999 and the [[Louisiana Sports Hall of Fame]] in 2000. He currently hosts an afternoon radio show on [[WWL (AM)|WWL]] [[AM 870]] and [[WWL-FM]] 105.3 in [[New Orleans]].

==Playing career==

===USFL===
Hebert was among the greatest quarterbacks in the USFL's short history. In 1983, he won the USFL championship with the [[Michigan Panthers]], defeating the [[Philadelphia/Baltimore Stars|Philadelphia Stars]], 24–22. The team struggled with injuries in 1984 and a weakened squad was knocked out of the playoffs by [[Steve Young]]'s [[Los Angeles Express (USFL)|Los Angeles Express]] 27–21 in triple overtime.  In 1985, the Panthers were merged with the Oakland Invaders and Hebert again led his team to the finals against the Stars. This time Hebert's team fell short and the Stars won 28–24. In three years in the USFL, Hebert completed 773 of 1,407 passes for 13,137 passing yards. He is the USFL's all-time leader in passing yardage.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://geocities.com/Colosseum/Arena/6925/usfl.html |title=Steve Dimitry's USFL Web Page |website=geocities.com |access-date=12 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091020034107/http://geocities.com/Colosseum/Arena/6925/usfl.html |archive-date=20 October 2009 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

USFLOnline.com: Hebert remembers when the Panthers were the “Talk-of-the-Town” in the city of Detroit. “We were a lot more popular than the Lions were,” he says. “We won the USFL Championship after Detroit not having a champion since the Bobby Layne days in the 1950s.”

Hebert, with a confident tone in his voice, says, “I think we would have been in the top 14 of the NFL if we [Panthers] played them. We didn't have the depth as the NFL, but we had a good chance to win because the guys that started on the Panthers also started in the NFL later on.”

===NFL===
In 1985, his rookie season with the [[National Football League|NFL]]'s [[New Orleans Saints]], and in 1986, he split time with quarterback [[Dave Wilson (American football)|Dave Wilson]]. In 1987, he was made starting quarterback with [[John Fourcade]] as backup. In week 12 of the 1988 NFL Season on November 20, Hebert completed 20 of 23 passes for 194 yards and 3 touchdown passes in the Saints' 42–0 rout over the [[Denver Broncos]], for his efforts he was named the Associated Press NFC Offensive Player of the week. Hebert sat out the entire 1990 season in a contract dispute. In 1991 and 1992 he led the Saints to excellent starts and impressive playoff appearances. Hebert was honored by gracing the front cover of the October 7, 1991 ''[[Sports Illustrated]]''.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://vault.si.com/vault/2004/06/07/catching-up-with-bobby-hebert-quarterback-october-7-1991 | title=Catching up with ... Bobby Hebert, Quarterback OCTOBER 7, 1991 }}</ref> In 1993, he was signed by the Atlanta Falcons and was selected for the [[Pro Bowl]] that season. He continued to play for the [[Atlanta Falcons]] as a backup to [[Jeff George]] in 1994 and 1995, and he was named starter again in 1996. Hebert retired after his 1996 season with the Falcons.

'''Robert Carl Hoying''' (born September 20, 1972) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[quarterback]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Ohio State Buckeyes football|Ohio State Buckeyes]]. He was selected in the third round of the [[1996 NFL draft]]. He is the grandson of baseball player [[Wally Post]], who played 15 years in the [[MLB|Major Leagues]].{{Citation needed|date=February 2024}}  Post was an outfielder for the [[Cincinnati Reds]] 1961 [[National League pennant]] winning team.

==Early life==
Hoying grew up in [[Mercer County, Ohio]], attending [[St. Henry High School]], where he won one [[high school football|football]] and two basketball state championships. He had college basketball offers from the University of Toledo and other colleges.

==College career==
Hoying played [[college football]] for the [[Ohio State University|Ohio State]] [[Ohio State Buckeyes football|Buckeyes]].  In 1993 as a sophomore he was named  starting quarterback, but shared snaps with Bret Powers a transfer from [[Arizona State University|Arizona State]].  By 1994, Hoying acquired a firm hold on the starting spot.

In his career at Ohio State Hoying completed 498 passes and 57 touchdown passes, both school records.  He is third behind [[J. T. Barrett]] and [[Art Schlichter]] on the Ohio State career passing yardage list.  He was an outstanding college student and was selected as an All Big 10 Scholar Athlete.

Hoying was selected to the [[Ohio State Varsity O Hall of Fame]] in 2008.

Hoying was [[NFL draft|drafted]] in the third round of the [[1996 NFL draft]] with the 85th overall pick by the [[Philadelphia Eagles]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1996 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1996/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-30 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> Hoying played well in two games in 1997 after taking over the starting role at midseason and throwing 11 touchdown passes. He won a memorable 44–42 shootout win over [[Boomer Esiason]] and the [[Cincinnati Bengals]] after throwing four touchdown passes.

The following year however, would be a complete disaster for Hoying as he was benched midseason after not winning a single game as a starter. He did not throw a touchdown pass and threw nine interceptions. The 3–13 season led to the firing of Eagles [[head coach]] [[Ray Rhodes]] and ultimately the hiring of [[Andy Reid]]. Reid drafted [[Donovan McNabb]] out of [[Syracuse Orange football|Syracuse]] and Hoying was traded to the [[Oakland Raiders]] in August 1999, rejoining coach [[Jon Gruden]] who had been the [[offensive coordinator]] for the Eagles under Rhodes.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://apnews.com/article/208dc8569aed57a6912caa808e30ec49|title=Eagles Trade Hoying to Oakland|website=apnews.com|access-date=2021-10-19}}</ref> Hoying served as a backup to [[Rich Gannon]] in his first season with Oakland. In 2000 Hoying would play in the [[AFC Championship Game]] against the [[Baltimore Ravens]] standing in for the injured Gannon, but his team lost the game 16-3. Hoying retired after the 2001 season following a severe elbow injury. He holds the NFL record for most pass completions in a season without a touchdown.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://pfref.com/tiny/wKFQQ|title=Player Season Finder}}</ref>

Since leaving professional football Hoying has become a principal at Crawford Hoying, a full-service real estate company based in Columbus, Ohio.<ref>Gary Kravitz, [http://www.philadelphiaeagles.com/news/Story-WhereAreTheyNow.asp?story_id=15342 "Where Are They Now: QB Bobby Hoying"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090311014209/http://www.philadelphiaeagles.com/news/Story-WhereAreTheyNow.asp?story_id=15342 |date=March 11, 2009 }} (April 19, 2008)</ref>

'''Bobby Hamilton''' (born July 1, 1971) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive end]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). Hamilton attended East Marion High School in Columbia, Mississippi and was a student and a [[Letterman (sports)|letterman]] in [[High school football|football]], [[basketball]], [[baseball]], and [[Track and field|track]]. Bobby Hamilton graduated from East Marion High School in 1989.

==College career==
Hamilton attended the [[University of Southern Mississippi]] and was a student and a football standout. In football, he was a four-year letterman and a two-year starter, and finished his impressive [[college football]] career with 18 [[Quarterback sack|sacks]] and 173 [[tackle (football move)|tackles]] (18 for losses).

'''Bobby Bryant''' (born January 24, 1944) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[cornerback]] who played for the [[Minnesota Vikings]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[South Carolina Gamecocks football|South Carolina Gamecocks]].

==Early life==
At Willingham High School, he was a star in football along with basketball, track and field, and baseball.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://bobbybryantviking.com/|title=Bobby Bryant, Minnesota Viking & Carolina Gamecock|website=bobbybryantviking.com}}</ref> Bryant was recruited to play for the [[University of South Carolina]] by Weems Baskin in 1963. Baskin was both the track coach and a football assistant, but Bryant (nicknamed "Bones" owing to his lanky frame) ended up playing both baseball and football, for which he would earn a letter for three years with each sport.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://gamecocksonline.com/news/2003/10/10/Where_Are_They_Now_Bobby_Bryant.aspx|title=Where Are They Now? Bobby Bryant|website=University of South Carolina Athletics|date=10 October 2003 }}</ref> He was awarded the [[ACC Athlete of the Year]] in 1967. He is the first and only athlete from South Carolina to have won the award along with the first Gamecock to have struck out 100 batters in a season. Bryant, who served as pitcher for the Gamecocks, was selected in the [[Major League Baseball]] Draft in his junior and senior seasons by the [[New York Yankees]] and the [[Boston Red Sox]], respectively, but he decided to play with the Vikings when they drafted him.

In his senior season, Bryant set a school record with a 98-yard punt return against [[North Carolina State]], assisting the team to a 31–21 win in what turned out to be their only victory of the year.  Bryant also had a 77-yard punt return the season opening game against LSU.  In 1979, Bryant was voted into the South Carolina athletic hall of fame.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://scfootballhof.org/inductees/inductees-2019/bobby-bryant/ | title=Bobby Bryant }}</ref>

==Football career==
After knee injury during the pre-season with the Vikings kept him on the team's practice squad in 1967, Bryant spent his rookie season with the [[Des Moines Warriors]] from the minor [[Professional Football League of America]] (PFLA). A season later he began his career with the Vikings in 1968, which was also the same year that [[Paul Krause]] was traded to the team. Together they would play with each other for twelve seasons, and they would combine for 104 interceptions (with nine combined interceptions in playoff games).

Bryant was used as both a defensive back and a returner on punts and kicks for his rookie season, and he soon became known for blowing kisses to the crowd.  He returned 19 kicks for 373 yards to go with ten punt returns for 49 yards. He had his first interception in his fourth game against the [[New Orleans Saints]] on October 13. He intercepted [[Billy Kilmer]] twice and returned one of the interceptions 51 yards for a touchdown.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/196810130nor.htm|title=Minnesota Vikings at New Orleans Saints - October 13th, 1968|website=Pro-Football-Reference.com}}</ref> They were the only interceptions of his rookie season, for which he made no starts at the position. Bryant, given more playing time on the defensive part of the field, improved readily in 1969. Playing in ten games, he made eight interceptions, which would prove to be a career high. He ranked second in interceptions in the NFL next to [[Lem Barney]] (8) and [[Mel Renfro]] (10). It was the first of four seasons that Bryant would finish in the top ten for interceptions. It was also the first of four times that he led the Vikings in interceptions.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1969/leaders.htm|title=1969 NFL Leaders and Leaderboards|website=Pro-Football-Reference.com}}</ref>

In the NFC Championship against the [[Dallas Cowboys]] on December 30, {{NFL Year|1973}}, he returned a [[Roger Staubach]] pass 63 yards for a touchdown, which was at the time the longest interception return for a touchdown by a Viking.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.profootballhof.com/hof/release.aspx?release_id=2959|title=Reed rumbles 108 yards for NFL record {{!}} Longest interception returns by team|work=[[Pro Football Hall of Fame]]|date=November 24, 2008|access-date=June 2, 2014}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/197312300dal.htm|title=NFC Championship - Minnesota Vikings at Dallas Cowboys - December 30th, 1973|website=Pro-Football-Reference.com}}</ref>

Bryant returned to full strength in 1975. He played in each game and recorded six interceptions (good for seventh in the league). He was named to his first Pro Bowl that year. In 1976, he recorded just two interceptions but was named to the Pro Bowl once again.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/B/BryaBo01.htm|title=Bobby Bryant 1976 Game Log|website=Pro-Football-Reference.com}}</ref> In the [[1976–77 NFL playoffs|1976 NFC Championship]] on December 26 against the [[Los Angeles Rams]], he scored the first points of the game when he returned a blocked [[Tom Dempsey]] field goal kick 90 yards for a touchdown. He also recorded two interceptions off [[Pat Haden]] as the Vikings rolled on to make their fourth Super Bowl in franchise history, with Bryant being one of just eleven Vikings to have played in each of those Super Bowls.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/197612260min.htm|title=NFC Championship - Los Angeles Rams at Minnesota Vikings - December 26th, 1976|website=Pro-Football-Reference.com}}</ref>

Bryant had his last peak with 1978, as he recorded seven interceptions (which ranked as more than he had in his last two seasons combined).
At the age of 36, Bryant played his last season in 1980. He did not record an interception for his first eight games, but he closed his career out with three in his last six games played, including his last one in the season finale against the Houston Oilers, doing so against [[Ken Stabler]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/B/BryaBo01.htm|title=Bobby Bryant 1980 Game Log|website=Pro-Football-Reference.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/198012210oti.htm|title=Minnesota Vikings at Houston Oilers - December 21st, 1980|website=Pro-Football-Reference.com}}</ref>

At the time of his retirement, Bryant ranked tenth all-time in interceptions, having become one of eighteen players at the time to have recorded 50 interceptions as a player. Since then, 21 have crossed the mark, and Bryant ranks 39th.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/leaders/def_int_career_1980.htm|title=NFL Career Interceptions Leaders Through 1980|website=Pro-Football-Reference.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/leaders/def_int_career.htm|title=NFL Interceptions Career Leaders (since 1940)|website=Pro-Football-Reference.com}}</ref> He is second in interceptions as a Viking (51) next to [[Paul Krause]].  He also intercepted another six passes in his 14 postseason games, including three in the Vikings Super Bowl season of 1976.

==Personal life==
In 1979, he was inducted into the University of South Carolina Athletic Hall of Fame. After retiring, he lived in Minnesota for five years before settling in [[Columbia, South Carolina]] and worked in sales for Harmon Autoglass, an auto glass replacement business.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://scfootballhof.org/inductees/inductees-2019/bobby-bryant/|title=Bobby Bryant|website=SC Football Hall of Fame | Become a life changer for our youth!}}</ref>

'''Bobbie Joe Williams Jr.''' (born September 25, 1976) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Guard (gridiron football)|guard]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Arkansas Razorbacks football|Arkansas Razorbacks]] and was selected by the [[Philadelphia Eagles]] in the second round of the [[2000 NFL draft]]. Williams also played for the [[Cincinnati Bengals]] and [[Baltimore Ravens]].

==Early life==
Williams attended [[Jefferson High School (Jefferson, Texas)|Jefferson High School]] in [[Jefferson, Texas]], and was a [[Letterman (sports)|letterman]] in [[High school football|football]], [[basketball]], and [[track and field]].  In football, he was named the East Texas Lineman of the Year as a senior.  In basketball, he was an All-Distinct honoree. He has a daughter, Tiana, who  attends [[University of Arkansas]] and a son, Brandon, who attends Rutgers University. He is known for being one of the kindest men in the NFL.

==College career==
Williams started at tackle for the last 25 games of his career at the [[Arkansas Razorbacks football|University of Arkansas]].  As a senior, Williams earned second-team [[List of All-SEC football teams|All-Southeastern Conference]] honors, playing on a line that led the SEC in fewest sacks allowed (14), while helping the offense amass 4067 total yards. Williams also helped the Arkansas Razorbacks beat the Texas Longhorns 27–6 in the 2000 Cotton Bowl Classic.

Williams majored in vocational training.

==Professional career==

===Philadelphia Eagles===
Williams was selected by the [[Philadelphia Eagles]] in the second round (61st overall) in the [[2000 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=2000 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2000/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-19 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He was inactive throughout the entire [[2000 NFL season|2000 season]] as he made the transition from tackle to guard. He made his NFL debut at the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] on January 6, 2001, starting at right guard. Williams played in every game for the Eagles in [[2002 NFL season|2002]] and [[2003 NFL season|2003]] and also played in two playoff games in 2002. He took over the starting right guard job after an elbow injury to [[Jermane Mayberry]] in 2003.
During his four years with Philadelphia, Williams helped the Eagles win three [[NFC East]] Division titles in a row (2001–2003), reaching the [[NFC Championship Game]] (2001–2003) during that three-year run.

===Cincinnati Bengals===
On March 26, 2004, Williams signed with the [[Cincinnati Bengals]] as an [[unrestricted free agent]].  He was the only player both on offense to play every snap on his unit. In 2005, Williams was part of the offensive line which only allowed 21 sacks which beat the previous franchise record of 24 sacks set in the 1972–73 season. He was re-signed to a two-year contract on April 5, 2010.<ref>{{cite web |author=Rosenthal, Gregg |title=Bobbie Williams' contract will be for two years |url=http://profootballtalk.nbcsports.com/2010/04/05/bobbie-williams-contract-will-be-for-two-years/ |publisher=[[Profootballtalk.com]] |date=April 5, 2010 |access-date=2010-04-05}}</ref> In Week 14 of the [[2011 NFL season]], Williams broke his ankle in a 20–19 loss against the [[Houston Texans]], causing him to miss the remainder of the season.<ref>{{cite web|title=Bobbie Williams Out for the Season, Maybe for Career|url=http://www.bengals101.com/2011/12/12/bobbie-williams-out-for-the-season-maybe-for-career/|access-date=2011-12-13|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120426051041/http://www.bengals101.com/2011/12/12/bobbie-williams-out-for-the-season-maybe-for-career/|archive-date=2012-04-26|url-status=dead}}</ref>
During his time in Cincinnati, Williams helped the Bengals win two [[AFC North]] Division titles (2005, 2009).

===Baltimore Ravens===
On June 8, 2012, Williams signed a two-year contract with the [[Baltimore Ravens]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Bobbie Williams agrees to deal, will compete for Ravens' LG job.| website=[[NFL.com]] |url=http://www.nfl.com/news/story/09000d5d829b0198/article/bobbie-williams-agrees-to-deal-will-compete-for-ravens-lg-job?module=HP11_headline_stack|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141129113653/http://www.nfl.com/news/story/09000d5d829b0198/article/bobbie-williams-agrees-to-deal-will-compete-for-ravens-lg-job?module=HP11_headline_stack|url-status=dead|archive-date=November 29, 2014}}</ref> He won his first career Super Bowl on February 3, 2013, when the Ravens defeated the San Francisco 49ers by a score of 34–31 in [[Super Bowl XLVII]]. He was a backup most of the season and started six games.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bobbie Williams 2012 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/W/WillBo21/gamelog/2012/ |access-date=2025-06-07 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>

On March 8, 2013, Williams was released by the Ravens.<ref>{{cite web | last=Hensley |first=Jamison |title=Ravens release Bobbie Williams |url=https://www.espn.com/blog/nflnation/post/_/id/73533/ravens-release-bobbie-williams |work=ESPN.com |date=March 8, 2013 |access-date=2013-03-08}}</ref>

'''Robert Theodore Trumpy Jr.''' (March 6, 1945 – November 2, 2025) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player and sports broadcaster. He was a [[tight end]] for the  [[Cincinnati Bengals]] of the [[American Football League]] (AFL) and [[National Football League]] (NFL) from 1968 through 1977. He was a two-time NFL [[Pro Bowl]]er and two-time [[American Football League All-Star game|AFL All-Star]].

Trumpy played [[college football]] for the [[Illinois Fighting Illini football|Illinois Fighting Illini]] and [[Utah Utes football|Utah Utes]] before being selected by the Bengals in the 12th round of the [[1968 NFL/AFL draft]]. After his playing career, Trumpy spent many years as a broadcast [[color analyst]], calling four [[Super Bowl]]s. He was given the [[Pete Rozelle Radio-Television Award]] by the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] in 2014.

== Early life ==
Robert Theodore Trumpy Jr. was born on March 6, 1945,<ref name=":0" />{{efn|name=birthplace|A Bengals media guide from Trumpy's tenure with the team in 1972 lists his "hometown" as [[Springfield, Illinois]],<ref name="mediaguide"/> while their 1977 guide lists his "birthplace" as Springfield.<ref>{{cite web |date=1977 |title=Cincinnati Bengals 1977 |page=32|url=https://archive.org/details/bengals-1977-media-guide-cincinnati-c/page/32/mode/2up |publisher=The Central Trust Company |access-date=November 4, 2025|via=Internet Archive}}</ref> Sources published in 1993 differ on whether he was born in [[Bloomington, Indiana]],<ref name=":6"/> or [[Bloomington, Illinois]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Herbert |first=Steven |date=January 31, 1993 |title=BOB TRUMPY: His Big Game Plan |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1993-01-31-tv-874-story.html |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |access-date=November 4, 2025}}</ref> ''[[The New York Times]]'' wrote in his obituary that he was born in [[Mount Pulaski, Illinois]].<ref name=sandomir_11042025/>}} and grew up in [[Tremont, Illinois]].<ref name=":6"/> When his father, Robert Sr. had a job transfer, his family moved from Tremont to [[Springfield, Illinois]]. He played multiple sports at [[Tremont High School]] and went to [[Springfield High School (Illinois)|Springfield High School]] as a sophomore. He was all-state in football and basketball.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Kane |first=Dave |date=February 22, 2014 |title=A gridiron great |url=https://www.sj-r.com/story/special/special-sections/2014/02/23/a-gridiron-great/38759854007/ |access-date=November 28, 2024 |website=The State Journal-Register |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=Trumpy, Bob (1983) |url=https://basketballmuseumofillinois.com/hall-of-fame/players/19-hof-players/1647-bob-trumpy/ |access-date=November 28, 2024 |website=Basketball Museum of Illinois |language=en-US}}</ref> He was on Springfield's state championship basketball team, and he was team captain as a senior there, as well as being named All-State.<ref name=":3" />

Bob Trumpy played in four state tournaments, which took place at the [[University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign]], during this time, two in basketball and two in track, where he won the 1963 state meet in long jump<ref name=":2" /> and tied for fifth in high jump.<ref>{{cite web |last=Mahan |first=Ryan |date=November 2, 2025 |title=Springfield grad Bob Trumpy, former Cincinnati tight end and NFL broadcaster, dead at 80 |url=https://www.sj-r.com/story/sports/nfl/2025/11/02/bob-trumpy-springfield-grad-pro-football-tight-end-dead-at-80/87054164007/ |publisher=The State Journal-Register |access-date=November 2, 2025}}</ref> He was inducted into the Basketball Museum of Illinois Hall of Fame in 1983.<ref name=":3" /> In 1991, he was among the first inductees into the Springfield Sports Hall of Fame, and in 1996 he was inducted into the Springfield High Hall of Fame.<ref name=":2" />

== College career ==
After graduation in 1963, Trumpy played college football at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.<ref name=":2" /> Since freshmen were not allowed to play on the [[varsity team]], his first season with the [[Illinois Fighting Illini football|Fighting Illini]] was in [[1964 Illinois Fighting Illini football team|1964]] playing as a [[wide receiver]], [[reception (gridiron football)|catching]] a team-high 28 passes for 428 yards and two [[touchdown]]s.<ref name=sandomir_11042025/><ref name=mahan_05022020/><ref name=":4">{{Cite web |title=Bob Trumpy College Stats, School, Draft, Gamelog, Splits |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/bob-trumpy-1.html |access-date=November 29, 2024 |website=College Football at Sports-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He missed the last two games of the season with a knee injury.<ref name=mahan_05022020/> Trumpy then transferred to the [[University of Utah]] in [[Salt Lake City]] which required him to miss the [[1965 Utah Redskins football team|1965 season]]. In [[1966 Utah Redskins football team|1966]], he converted to the tight end position, catching nine passes for 159 yards and two scores for the [[Utah Utes football|Utes]].<ref name=":4" /> Afterwards, he dropped out of school.<ref name=sandomir_11042025/>

Trumpy briefly studied at Glendale Junior College (now [[Glendale Community College (California)|Glendale Community College]]) in [[Los Angeles County, California|Los Angeles County]]. After joining the [[United States Navy Reserve|United States Naval Reserve]],<ref name=sandomir_11042025/> he was activated into the [[United States Navy|Navy]], serving 180 days during the [[Vietnam War]].<ref name=mahan_05022020>{{Cite web |last=Mahan |first=Ryan |date=May 2, 2020 |title=From Springfield to the pros, Bengals' Bob Trumpy remains gold standard |url=https://www.sj-r.com/story/sports/nfl/2020/05/02/from-springfield-to-pros-bengals/1251960007/ |access-date=March 19, 2024 |website=The State Journal-Register |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Professional career ==
After being discharged from the Navy, Trumpy worked briefly as a bill collector before being selected by the AFL's [[1968 Cincinnati Bengals season|Bengals]] in the [[1968 NFL/AFL draft#Round twelve|12th round]] (301st overall) of the [[1968 NFL/AFL draft|1968 common draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1968 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1968/draft.htm |access-date=November 28, 2024 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> Despite his low draft selection, Trumpy worked hard in the offseason and managed to earn the starting tight end spot in the team's lineup. He didn't disappoint in his rookie season, recording 37 receptions for 639 yards and three touchdowns,<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Bob Trumpy Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/T/TrumBo00.htm |access-date=November 28, 2024 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> and earning a place on the [[American Football League All-Star game|AFL Western Division All-Star]] team.<ref name=":0" /> In Cincinnati, Trumpy played under [[Pro Football Hall of Fame|hall of fame]] coach [[Paul Brown]], head coach [[Bill Johnson (center)|Tiger Johnson]], and offensive coach [[Bill Walsh]], another hall of fame coach and offensive innovator.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Hobson |first=Geoff |date=May 19, 2018 |title=TDBH: Tight end trend-setter Trumpy retires to start another |url=https://www.bengals.com/news/tdbh-tight-end-trend-setter-trumpy-retires-to-start-another-20466872 |access-date=November 28, 2024 |website=www.bengals.com |language=en-US}}</ref>

In [[1969 Cincinnati Bengals season|1969]], Trumpy averaged 22.6 yards per catch, on 37 passes for 835 yards and nine touchdowns.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":0" /> He was selected first-team [[American Football League All-League Team|AFL All-League tight end]] by numerous entities, including the [[Associated Press]] (AP), [[Pro Football Weekly]], the [[Newspaper Enterprise Association]] (NEA), and [[United Press International]] (UPI), and second-team by ''[[The Sporting News]]'' and the [[Pro Football Writers of America|Professional Football Writers of America]].<ref name=":0" /> He was again selected to the AFL All-Star team.<ref name=":0" /> In a November 1969 game against the [[Houston Oilers]], Trumpy became the first Bengals tight end to record three touchdown receptions in a single game, helping his team to a 31–31 tie.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cincinnati Bengals at Houston Oilers - November 9th, 1969 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/196911090oti.htm |access-date=November 28, 2024 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> In [[1970 Cincinnati Bengals season|1970]], with the Bengals now part of the [[National Football League]] following the AFL-NFL merger, ''The Sporting News'' and AP selected him first-team AFC All-Conference.<ref name=":0" />

Trumpy earned two trips to the [[Pro Bowl]] in 1970 and 1973 and continued to play for the Bengals until [[1977 NFL season|1977]]. In his final season, he caught only 18 passes for 251 yards and one touchdown,<ref name=":0" /> but his touchdown was one of the most memorable plays of his career. In a November 20 game against the [[Miami Dolphins]] during a driving rainstorm, Trumpy caught a 29-yard touchdown pass from quarterback [[Ken Anderson (quarterback)|Ken Anderson]] on a [[flea flicker]] play that involved three players handling the ball before it was thrown to him.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Pregame Notebook: Few Words Needed For Old Steeler Hilton As Bengals Brace For WR Johnson |url=https://www.bengals.com/news/pregame-notebook-few-words-needed-for-old-steeler-hilton-as-bengals-brace-for-wr |access-date=November 29, 2024 |website=www.bengals.com |language=en-US}}</ref> First, Anderson handed the ball off to running back [[Archie Griffin]], who then pitched the ball to receiver [[John McDaniel (American football)|John McDaniel]] running in the opposite direction. McDaniel then handed the ball back to Anderson, setting up his 29-yard touchdown pass to Trumpy.<ref>{{cite news |last=Harmon |first=Pat |date=November 21, 1977 |title=Here's the magic that kept Cincinnati in the race |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-cincinnati-post-heres-the-magic-tha/184202384/ |publisher=Cincinnati Post |access-date=November 2, 2025}}</ref> The Bengals went on to defeat the Dolphins 23–17, knocking them out of playoff contention.<ref>{{cite news |last=Harmon |first=Pat |date=November 21, 1977 |title=Bengals go back 10 years for play that beat Miami 
|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-cincinnati-post-bengals-go-back-10-y/184202650/ |publisher=Cincinnati Post |access-date=November 2, 2025}}</ref> <!-- (Unsourced quote, please find ref) "It was magic", said Trumpy about the play, {{cquote|[[Don Shula]] (the Dolphins coach at the time) reminds me of that play every time I see him. He called it 'triple pass' because 3 people touched it before I caught it, but Shula called it the reverse pass. He'll see me and say 'That damn reverse pass. I remember that.'}} -->

== Broadcasting career ==
While not a Hall of Fame player, Trumpy had a Hall of Fame broadcasting career. He called four Super Bowls, four Pro Bowls, six Hall-of-Fame Games in football in addition to three [[Ryder Cup]]s and three [[Olympic Games|Olympics]].<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":5" /> Trumpy's first broadcast experience was in 1964, working with Coley Cowan on a [[WTAX (AM)|WTAX]] in a [[Springfield, Illinois]] radio broadcast of a basketball tournament in Springfield.<ref name=":2" /> After retiring, he joined [[WCKY (AM)|WCKY]] radio as a sports talk host.<ref name=":1" />

Trumpy expanded into NFL broadcasting in 1978, joining [[NFL on NBC|NBC]] as a [[color analyst]] for telecasts of [[American Football Conference|AFC]] games, primarily working with [[Sam Nover]] through 1980, then with [[Bob Costas]]<ref>{{Cite web |last=Goodykoontz |first=Bill |title=The best NFL broadcast teams of all time |url=https://www.azcentral.com/picture-gallery/entertainment/media/2020/09/11/best-nfl-announcers/3468738001/ |access-date=November 29, 2024 |website=The Arizona Republic |language=en-US}}</ref> (1981-1983), and [[Don Criqui]] (1984–1988).<ref>{{Cite web |date=September 29, 2017 |title=Former NBC announcer Bob Trumpy has fond memories of Browns and Bengals games |url=https://www.espn.com/blog/cleveland/post/_/id/3969/former-nbc-announcer-bob-trumpy-has-fond-memories-of-browns-and-bengals-games |access-date=November 28, 2024 |website=ESPN.com |language=en}}</ref> Trumpy and Criqui also served as [[NFL on NBC Radio|NBC Radio]]'s lead NFL announcers from 1985 to 1986, calling ''[[Monday Night Football#Radio broadcasts|Monday Night Football]]'' and Super Bowls [[Super Bowl XX|XX]] and [[Super Bowl XXI|XXI]].<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |title=Bob Trumpy named Rozelle Award winner {{!}} Pro Football Hall of Fame |url=https://www.profootballhof.com/news/2014/07/news-bob-trumpy-named-rozelle-award-winner/ |access-date=November 29, 2024 |website=pfhof |language=en}}</ref> In 1992, Trumpy replaced [[Bill Walsh]] as NBC's lead NFL analyst,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Cwik |first=Chris |date=November 2, 2025 |title=Bob Trumpy, former Bengals tight end and broadcaster, dies at 80 |url=https://sports.yahoo.com/nfl/breaking-news/article/bob-trumpy-former-bengals-tight-end-and-broadcaster-dies-at-80-182308192.html |website=Yahoo Sports |access-date=November 3, 2025}}</ref> teaming with [[Dick Enberg]] until 1995 (when NBC went to a three-man booth with [[Paul Maguire]] and [[Phil Simms]] replacing him).<ref name="nyt_06291995" /> The team of Enberg and Trumpy called Super Bowls [[Super Bowl XXVII|XXVII]] (1993) and [[Super Bowl XXVIII|XXVIII]] (1994).<ref name=":5" /> He was paired with [[Tom Hammond]] (1995–1996)<ref name="nyt_06291995">{{cite news |date=June 29, 1995 |title=SPORTS PEOPLE: TV SPORTS; Trumpy Off NBC's Top Unit |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1995/06/29/sports/sports-people-tv-sports-trumpy-off-nbc-s-top-unit.html |work=[[New York Times]] |access-date=November 2, 2025}}</ref> and [[Charlie Jones (sportscaster)|Charlie Jones]] (1997)<ref>{{cite news |last=Stewart |first=Larry |date=September 26, 1997 |title=NBC Couldn't Say 'Yes' to Guilty Albert |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1997-sep-26-sp-36482-story.html |newspaper=[[LA Times]] |access-date=November 2, 2025}}</ref> until NBC lost the AFC broadcasting package to [[NFL on CBS|CBS]] following the 1997 season.<ref>{{cite web |author=[[Associated Press]] |date=November 2, 2025 |title=Bob Trumpy, former All-Pro tight end with Bengals and longtime broadcaster, dies at age of 80 |url=https://www.nfl.com/news/bob-trumpy-dies-age-80-former-all-pro-tight-end-bengals-broadcaster |publisher=[[NFL]] |access-date=November 2, 2025}}</ref>

Trumpy hosted a weeknight [[Sports radio|sports talk show]] on [[WLW-AM]] in [[Cincinnati]] (1980–1989), and was Ohio Sports Broadcaster of the Year four times.<ref name=":2" /> He left the show to be able to work more assignments at [[NBC Sports]], including [[PGA Tour on NBC|PGA Tour]] golf and the [[Olympics on NBC|Olympics]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Trumpy to leave WLW for NBC |url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1989/12/19/Trumpy-to-leave-WLW-for-NBC/1474630046800/ |access-date=November 29, 2024 |website=UPI |language=en}}</ref> He was replaced on the sports talk show by [[Cris Collinsworth]].<ref>{{cite web |last=McAlister |first=Lance |date=May 10, 2022 |title=Sports Talk Flashback: Cris Collinsworth as guest host Sports Talk, 1983 |url=https://espn1530.iheart.com/featured/lance-mcalister/content/2022-05-09-sports-talk-flashback-cris-collinsworth-as-guest-host-sports-talk-1983/ |publisher=Cincinnati's ESPN 1530 |access-date=November 2, 2025}}</ref>

On the night of November 10, 1983, while he was hosting his talk show on WLW, the first call that he received was from a despondent woman who said that she wanted to commit suicide. Trumpy spoke to the woman (and, later, her son) for more than two hours until the son gave him their address. He then spoke to the woman and her son for several more minutes after that until his station manager took him off the air. Police in [[Forest Park, Ohio]], went to the address that the son had given and took the woman to a local hospital. Trumpy received praise for his actions from the Forest Park police and suicide prevention counselors.<ref>{{cite web | title=Former Cincinnati Bengals tight end Bob Trumpy, now a... | website=UPI | date=November 11, 1983 | url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1983/11/11/Former-Cincinnati-Bengals-tight-end-Bob-Trumpy-now-a/6390437374800/ | access-date=September 24, 2025}}</ref> He later said that he had to go to therapy because of the incident.<ref>Larry Stewart, [https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1993-01-29-sp-1904-story.html "Not Just Blowing Smoke, Trumpy Says He's Nervous"], ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'' (January 29, 1993).  Retrieved December 23, 2022.</ref>

Trumpy was an analyst for ''[[NFL on Westwood One Sports#Sunday Night Football|Sunday Night Football]]'' on [[NFL on Westwood One Sports|Westwood One]] radio from 2000 to 2007,<ref name=":2" /> save for the 2005 season, when he was replaced by [[John Riggins]].<ref>{{cite web |date=April 19, 2024 <!--Despite the last date updated, all the info regards the 2005 NFL season--> |title="Sportscasting in the News" |url=http://www.americansportscastersonline.com/asa-sportsbeat.html |publisher=ASA Sportsbeat |access-date=November 2, 2025}}</ref> During the first round of the [[2006-07 NFL playoffs]], Trumpy and Enberg were in the broadcast booth together for the first time since the [[1994–95 NFL playoffs#AFC Championship: San Diego Chargers 17.2C Pittsburgh Steelers 13|1994 AFC Championship Game]], covering the [[NFL playoffs, 2006-07#AFC: Indianapolis Colts 23.2C Kansas City Chiefs 8|Colts–Chiefs game]] for Westwood One.<ref>{{cite press release |date=January 2, 2007 |title=THEY'RE HERE! PLAYOFFS KICK OFF WITH WILD CARD WEEKEND |url=https://www.nfl.info/nflmedia/w_releases/2006w%20releases/Capsules/WC%20FINAL.pdf |publisher=NFL |access-date=November 2, 2025}}</ref>  Trumpy was named the 2014 recipient of the [[Pete Rozelle Radio-Television Award]], given by the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] for lifetime achievement in NFL broadcasting.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{cite web |last=Kiesewetter |first=John |date=July 8, 2014 |title=Bob Trumpy: NFL Hall of Fame 'never crossed my mind' |url=https://www.cincinnati.com/story/tvandmediablog/2014/07/08/bob-trumpy-nfl-pro-football-hall-of-fame-pete-rozelle-concussions-nbc-wlw-am-wcky-am/12376991/ |publisher=Cincinnati Enquirer |access-date=November 2, 2025}}</ref>
