'''Bobby E. Abrams Jr.''' (born April 12, 1967) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL).  He played [[college football]] as a [[defensive back]] and linebacker for the [[Michigan Wolverines football|Michigan Wolverines]] from 1986 to 1989.  He played in the NFL for six seasons as a linebacker and [[special teams]] player for the [[New York Giants]] ([[1990 NFL season|1990]]–[[1992 NFL season|1992]], [[Cleveland Browns]] ([[1992 NFL season|1992]]), [[Dallas Cowboys]] ([[1992 NFL season|1992]]–[[1993 NFL season|1993]]), [[Minnesota Vikings]] ([[1993 NFL season|1993]]–[[1994 NFL season|1994]]) and [[New England Patriots]] ([[1995 NFL season|1995]]). He won three [[Super Bowl]] titles with the Giants and the Cowboys, all over the [[Buffalo Bills]].

==Early life==
Abrams was born in [[Detroit, Michigan]], in 1967. He attended [[Henry Ford High School (Detroit, Michigan)|Henry Ford High School]] in Detroit.<ref name="PFR">{{Cite web |title=Bobby Abrams |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/A/AbraBo20.htm |access-date=April 2, 2018 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |publisher=Sports Reference LLC}}</ref> He was an All-state selection as a senior. He made the honor roll for 8 straight semesters. He also practiced track.

==College career==
Abrams accepted a football scholarship from the [[University of Michigan]], to play under head coach [[Bo Schembechler]]'s [[Michigan Wolverines football]] teams from 1986 to 1989.<ref name="Roster">{{Cite web |title=All-Time Football Roster Database |url=https://bentley.umich.edu/athdept/rosters/football.php |access-date=April 1, 2018 |publisher=University of Michigan, Bentley Historical Library}}</ref> He began as a [[Safety (gridiron football position)|safety]] and was converted into a [[linebacker]] in spring drills in 1987.

As a sophomore, he was named the starter at right outside linebacker in the fourth game of the season. He started nine games (seven at outside linebacker, two at inside linebacker) for the [[1987 Michigan Wolverines football team]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1987 Michigan Football Team |url=https://bentley.umich.edu/athdept/football/fbteam/1987fbt.htm |access-date=April 1, 2018 |publisher=University of Michigan, Bentley Historical Library}}</ref>

As a redshirt junior, he started all 12 games at outside linebacker for the [[1988 Michigan Wolverines football team|1988 Michigan team]] that compiled a 9-2-1 record, won the [[Big Ten Conference]] championship, defeated USC in the [[1989 Rose Bowl]], and finished the season ranked #4 in the final [[AP Poll]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1988 Michigan Football Team |url=https://bentley.umich.edu/athdept/football/fbteam/1988fbt.htm |access-date=April 1, 2018 |publisher=University of Michigan, Bentley Historical Library}}</ref>

In his final year at Michigan, he again started all 12 games at outside linebacker for the [[1989 Michigan Wolverines football team|1989 Michigan team]] that compiled a 10–2 record, won a second consecutive Big Ten championship, lost to USC in the [[1990 Rose Bowl]], and finished the season ranked #7 in the final [[AP Poll]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1989 Michigan Football Team |url=https://bentley.umich.edu/athdept/football/fbteam/1989fbt.htm |access-date=April 1, 2018 |publisher=University of Michigan, Bentley Historical Library}}</ref> Against the [[University of Maryland]], he made 8 tackles, 3 sacks, one pass defensed and one fumble recovery.

==Professional career==
Abrams was signed as an [[undrafted free agent]] by the [[New York Giants]] after the [[1990 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=George |first=Thomas |date=August 15, 1991 |title=Abrams Fits the Mold Of Giants Linebacker |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1991/08/15/sports/football-abrams-fits-the-mold-of-giants-linebacker.html |access-date=January 25, 2018}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Abrams trying to fill Taylor's shoes |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1982&dat=19900807&id=z1ZGAAAAIBAJ&sjid=nSMNAAAAIBAJ&pg=4776,858435&hl=en |access-date=January 25, 2018}}</ref> As a rookie, he was a part of the [[Super Bowl XXV]] winning team. He was a [[special teams]] player and a backup linebacker behind [[Lawrence Taylor]] and [[Carl Banks]].<ref name=PFR/><ref>{{Cite news |date=August 20, 1992 |title=There are plenty of candidates for Banks' job |page=C7 |work=The Day |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1915&dat=19920820&id=rZRGAAAAIBAJ&sjid=JPgMAAAAIBAJ&pg=2396,4088270&hl=en}}</ref><ref name=NE/> He appeared in 32 games, including two as a starter in place of an injured Banks, before being waived on August 31, 1992.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Giants Cut Anderson, Reasons |url=https://www.courant.com/1992/09/01/giants-cut-anderson-reasons/ |access-date=January 25, 2018}}</ref>

On September 1, 1992, he was claimed by the [[Dallas Cowboys]] to provide depth on the [[special teams]] units. He had 4 [[special teams]] tackles and was cut on October 6.<ref>{{Cite news |date=October 7, 1992 |title=Transactions |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1992/10/07/sports/transactions-956092.html |access-date=January 25, 2018}}</ref> He was later signed by the [[Cleveland Browns]] where he played in three games. On November 9, he was claimed off waivers by the Giants after Taylor was lost for the year.<ref name=NE/><ref>{{Cite web |title=Subbing For Superman |url=https://www.courant.com/1992/11/12/subbing-for-superman/ |access-date=January 25, 2018}}</ref> On November 21, he was released to make room for [[Ken Willis]].<ref>{{Cite news |date=November 22, 1992 |title=Transactions |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1992/11/22/sports/transactions-704092.html |access-date=January 25, 2018}}</ref>

In April 1993, he was re-signed by the Cowboys. He joined the [[Minnesota Vikings]] for the last four games. The next year, he appeared in all 16 games for the Vikings as a backup, while leading the team with 28 special teams tackles.<ref name=PFR/><ref name="NE">{{Cite news |date=March 2, 1995 |title=Abrams signs with New England |page=D2 |work=Bangor Daily News |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=2457&dat=19950302&id=3qpJAAAAIBAJ&sjid=AA4NAAAAIBAJ&pg=4750,461004&hl=en}}</ref>

Abrams signed with the [[New England Patriots]] on March 1, 1995,<ref name=NE/> appearing in nine games (one start) during the season.<ref name=PFR/> On September 10, 1996, he was released from the [[injured reserve list]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Transactions |url=http://articles.baltimoresun.com/1996-09-11/sports/1996255085_1_active-roster-triple-a-contract |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130622050356/http://articles.baltimoresun.com/1996-09-11/sports/1996255085_1_active-roster-triple-a-contract |url-status=dead |archive-date=June 22, 2013 |access-date=January 25, 2018}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Abrams was a teacher and head coach at Southside High School. He is currently the principal at [[Jefferson Davis High School (Montgomery, Alabama)|Jefferson Davis High School]] in [[Montgomery, Alabama]]. His father Bobby Sr., is a former 3-time [[Golden Gloves]] boxing champion in Detroit.

'''Robert Gilchrist Douglass''' (born June 22, 1947) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[quarterback]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL), primarily with the [[Chicago Bears]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Kansas Jayhawks football|Kansas Jayhawks]] before being selected by the Bears in the second round of the [[1969 NFL/AFL draft]]. During his career, he also played for the [[San Diego Chargers]], the [[New Orleans Saints]], and the [[Green Bay Packers]]. Douglass retired after the 1978 season, after playing 10 seasons in the NFL.

==Early life==
Douglass was raised in [[El Dorado, Kansas]], where his father was a football coach.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.eldoradobaseballhof.org/hall/bobby-douglass.php|title=Bobby Douglass, Post 81 American Legion|work=El Dorado Baseball Hall of Fame and Museum|access-date=25 March 2013|archive-date=4 May 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180504011146/http://www.eldoradobaseballhof.org/hall/bobby-douglass.php|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==College career==
Playing at the [[University of Kansas]], Douglass was a two-time All-Big Eight Conference (1967–68) selection and an [[All-America college football team|All-American]] in 1968. During his senior season, he directed the [[Kansas Jayhawks football|Jayhawks]] to a 9–2 record, a share of the Big Eight Conference title and a spot in the 1969 Orange Bowl. He passed for 1,316 yards and 12 touchdowns during his final year as a Jayhawk and finished seventh in the [[Heisman Trophy]] voting that season.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.kuathletics.com/sports/m-footbl/spec-rel/031011aaa.html|title=Former Kansas Quarterback Bobby Douglass Up for Induction to College Football Hall of Fame|author=KU Athletics Football|date=March 10, 2011|work=Official Website for the University of Kansas Athletics Department|access-date=October 20, 2011|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120609120435/http://www.kuathletics.com/sports/m-footbl/spec-rel/031011aaa.html|archive-date=June 9, 2012}}</ref>

==Professional career==
In 1972, playing for the [[Chicago Bears]], Douglass set the record for most rushing yards by a quarterback in one season. The record stood for 34 years. In a 14-game [[1972 NFL season|1972 season]], he ran for 968 yards and 8 [[Touchdown|touchdowns]] on 141 carries. Three quarterbacks in the NFL ([[Lamar Jackson]] twice, [[Michael Vick]], and [[Justin Fields]]) have since run for over 1,000 yards. With Douglass starting, the Chicago Bears had a 13–31–1 record.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://chicago.sbnation.com/2010/8/31/1657421/bears-quarterback-controversy-jay-cutler-bobby-douglass|title=Bobby Douglass: A Bears Quarterback Who Was One Of A Kind|author=Yellon, Al|date=August 31, 2010|work=SB Nation Chicago|access-date=October 25, 2011}}</ref>

In a November 4, 1973 game against the Packers, Douglass ran for four touchdowns in a 31–17 win. He and [[Billy Kilmer]] are the only quarterbacks in NFL history to rush for four touchdowns in a single game.

In five seasons from 1971 to 1975, Douglass played in 47 games and amassed 2,040 rushing yards. During that span, he averaged 43.4 rushing yards per game played—the third highest rushing yards per game average over a five-season span for a quarterback. ([[Michael Vick]] ranks first with 54.1 yards per game over a five-year span from 2002 to 2006). However, Douglass had little success as a passer, going 507-for-1178 for 36 touchdowns and 64 [[Interception|interceptions]] with a quarterback [[passer rating]] of only 48.5 during his 10-season NFL career.

'''Bobby Gene Humphrey''' (born October 11, 1966) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] for the [[Denver Broncos]] and [[Miami Dolphins]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Alabama Crimson Tide football|Alabama Crimson Tide]], twice earning [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] honors.

==College career==
Humphrey played from 1985 to 1988 for the [[Alabama Crimson Tide football|Crimson Tide]]. During his freshman year, he would share the backfield with Gene Jelks and Kerry Goode. He would rush for 502 yards, on 99 carries, and 4 touchdowns. During his sophomore year, he led the Crimson Tide in rushing with 1,471 yards and scored 15 touchdowns. The season ended on Christmas Day in the [[Sun Bowl]] against the [[Washington Huskies]]. Humphrey scored three touchdowns, and the Tide finished with a 10–3 record. He was named to an All-American team. In 1987, Bobby Humphrey was once again the featured back for the Tide. Rushing for 1,255 yards on 238 carries, and 11 touchdowns. One of the highlights of his junior year, was a 220-yard rushing performance against [[Penn State]]. On Halloween night, against [[Mississippi State]] he would pass [[Johnny Musso]] as Alabama's all-time leading rusher. Alabama would finish the year in the [[1988 Hall of Fame Bowl]], where Humphrey would score two touchdowns in a losing effort. He was once again named to an All-American team, and finished tenth in the [[Heisman Trophy]] voting. During spring practice, he would break his left foot. He started his senior season against [[Temple]], scoring a touchdown. But two weeks later, he would break his foot again ending his college career. He finished with 3,420 rushing yards and 33 touchdowns. At the end of his college career, no Alabama running back had more 200 yard rushing games, with four, and more 100 yard rushing games, with sixteen, than Bobby Humphrey.

In his four seasons playing for the Crimson Tide, Humphrey rushed for 3,420 yards (a school record at the time), caught 60 passes for 523 yards, and scored 40 touchdowns.  He made the [[College Football All-America Team]] in 1986 and 1987.  In 1986, he set a school record with 1,471 rushing yards.  In 1987, he was voted as UPI's offensive player of the year and finished 10th in the [[Heisman Trophy]] balloting.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.rolltide.com/fls/8000/files/football/records/All_Americans.pdf |title=Archived copy |accessdate=November 9, 2011 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110927224423/http://www.rolltide.com/fls/8000/files/football/records/All_Americans.pdf |archivedate=September 27, 2011 }}</ref>

==Professional career==
Humphrey was one of five players selected in the 1989 NFL [[NFL Draft#Supplemental draft|Supplemental Draft]], selected in the first round by the [[Denver Broncos]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1989 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1989/draft.htm |access-date=2023-05-27 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> During his rookie season, he rushed for 1,151 yards and seven touchdowns for the Broncos; he also threw a 17-yard touchdown pass and hauled in a touchdown reception. The Broncos qualified for [[Super Bowl XXIV]], but were defeated 55–10 by the [[San Francisco 49ers]].  Humphrey, although finishing the game as the Broncos leader in both rushing (61 yards) and receiving (31 yards), had a key turnover in the first quarter when he fumbled near midfield. Following this fumble, the 49ers would score 34 unanswered points to put the game away.  He followed his rookie season with a [[Pro Bowl]] selection in [[1991 Pro Bowl|1990]], rushing for 1,202 yards and seven touchdowns in [[1990 NFL season|1990]]. Humphrey was the first Denver Bronco to rush for 1,000 yards in back-to-back seasons.{{cn|date=November 2025}}

In [[1991 NFL season|1991]], Humphrey held out of training camp in hopes of obtaining a new contract.  The Broncos, by team policy, refused to renegotiate his pay and the holdout continued late into the season. Unable to secure a new contract, Humphrey finally ended his holdout in week 14.  However, by that time, newly signed [[Gaston Green]] had emerged as the team's starting running back and was on his way to completing his own 1,000-yard season.  Furthermore, Humphrey had fallen out of favor with the team's coaching and front office as a result of the holdout.  When Humphrey returned in week 14, he was out of shape and given only a reserve role in the Broncos' offense.  He remained on the bench as Denver made a run to the [[AFC Championship Game]], losing to the [[Buffalo Bills]] 10–7.

The following offseason, Humphrey was traded to the [[Miami Dolphins]] in exchange for running back [[Sammie Smith]].  He played for the Dolphins in [[1992 NFL season|1992]] scoring only one rushing touchdown and running for 471 yards; he also finished with 507 receiving yards and a touchdown reception. With his new team, Humphrey returned to the AFC Championship Game for the second consecutive season, losing again to the Buffalo Bills. After being out of football for two seasons, Humphrey attempted a comeback in 1995 with the Bills, but failed to make the team.

==Arena football coaching career==
In August 1999, the [[Birmingham Steeldogs]] formed as part of a new indoor football league called [[AF2]], a developmental league for the [[Arena Football League]]. Humphrey, with no coaching experience at that level, was named head coach. Over the course of six seasons, Humphrey guided the Steeldogs to a 51–50 record. After a disappointing 2–14 season, Humphrey was dismissed in 2005. The Steeldogs would rename themselves as the [[Alabama Steeldogs]] one year later, before ceasing operations following the 2007 season. The league would fold in 2009. Humphrey, at the time of his dismissal, was the second-winningest coach in the league.

==Post-football activities==
In 1998, Humphrey returned to the University of Alabama, and earned a bachelor's degree in social work. In 2004, he was inducted into the [[Alabama Sports Hall of Fame]]. During his time coaching in [[AF2]], he owned and operated Humphrey Construction Company. As of 2012, Humphrey is vice president of business development for Bryant Bank in [[Birmingham, Alabama]].<ref>[http://blog.al.com/press-register-sports/2009/05/former_alabama_great_bobby_hum.html Herndon: Former Alabama great Bobby Humphrey is watching a new No. 26 these days | al.com<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref> He was appointed to the City of Hoover's Parks and Recreation Board in 2014. In the summer of 2016, Humphrey was one of 75 players to be eligible for the 2017 Class for the College Football Hall of Fame.

==Personal life==
Humphrey is married. He and his wife Barbara have five children. Two of his sons have gone on to play college football. Maudrecus Humphrey played for the [[University of Arkansas]] and [[The University of Alabama at Birmingham|UAB]]. [[Marlon Humphrey]] followed his father's footsteps and played for Alabama, donning his father's jersey number 26, before being selected 16th overall by the [[Baltimore Ravens]] in the [[2017 NFL draft]].

==Shooting incident==
In February 1993, Humphrey was shot in his right thigh by friend and former teammate Mark Petties on an Alabama highway. Humphrey and Petties were returning from New Orleans, driving northbound on Interstate 65 in Humphrey's vehicle, when a fight ensued. The origin of the dispute was never made clear. A passing motorist saw the two fighting on the highway shoulder in Alabaster, AL, and called local police. When they arrived, Humphrey, 26, was lying on the ground. Humphrey was treated at Shelby Medical Center and released hours after the bullet was removed.

Eight days before the shooting incident, Humphrey had been arrested for cocaine possession, aggravated assault and destruction of hotel property in Columbus, GA.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.tampabay.com/archive/1993/02/09/dolphins-humphrey-shot-in-leg/ |title = Dolphins' Humphrey shot in leg}}</ref>

'''Robert Calvin Butler''' (born May 28, 1959) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[cornerback]] for the [[Atlanta Falcons]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). Butler played [[college football]] for the [[Florida State Seminoles football|Florida State Seminoles]]. Butler also competed for the [[Florida State Seminoles track and field]] team as a sprinter.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nolefan.org/garnet/seminole88.html|title=Stars of Yesterday: Bobby Butler, The First Great Cornerback|website=nolefan.org}}</ref>

Butler was selected in the first round of the [[1981 NFL draft]] by the Falcons. He played 12 seasons in the NFL, all with the Falcons, retiring after the 1992 season.<ref name=falcons.com />

Butler was inducted into the Seminoles' Hall of Fame in 1987.<ref name=tallahassee />

'''Robert Joseph Carpenter III''' (born August 1, 1983) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] for seven seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL), primarily with the [[Dallas Cowboys]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Ohio State Buckeyes football|Ohio State Buckeyes]], and was selected by the Cowboys in the first round of the [[2006 NFL draft]]. He also played in the NFL for the [[Miami Dolphins]], the [[Detroit Lions]] and the [[New England Patriots]].

==Early life==
Carpenter attended [[Lancaster High School (Ohio)|Lancaster High School]] in [[Lancaster, Ohio]], alma mater of [[Super Bowl]] champion [[Jim Cordle]].<ref name="Agonis">{{Cite web |last=Wilson |first=Tom |date=2023-08-31 |title=The Agonis Club names Bobby Carpenter Person of the Year and honors his family |url=https://www.lancastereaglegazette.com/story/sports/local/2023/08/30/the-agonis-club-names-bobby-carpenter-person-of-the-year-and-honors-his-family/70675279007/ |access-date=2025-08-07 |website=Lancaster Eagle Gazette}}</ref> In addition to being a [[High school football|football]] standout, he was also a member of the [[swimming (sport)|swim]] team. During his senior year, Carpenter was selected All-Ohio first-team in football, and also went to the District Finals in swimming.

==College career==
In 50 games at [[Ohio State Buckeyes football|Ohio State]], Carpenter started 26 times. He registered 191 tackles (121 solos), 14.5 sacks and 23.5 for losses, two forced fumbles, seven passes deflected passes and three interceptions.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Gutridge|first=Matt|date=2019-08-10|title=Countdown: 21 Days Until Ohio State Football|url=https://www.elevenwarriors.com/forum/ohio-state-football/2019/08/105832/countdown-21-days-until-ohio-state-football|access-date=2020-07-27|website=Eleven Warriors|language=en}}</ref>

In [[2002 Ohio State Buckeyes football team|2002]], Carpenter played in every game as a true freshman.<ref>{{cite web | title=Ohio State Football All Decade Team: A.J. Hawk, Bobby Carpenter | website=Land-Grant Holy Land|publisher=SB Nation | date=2013-06-22 | url=https://www.landgrantholyland.com/2013/6/22/4439830/ohio-state-football-all-decade-team-a-j-hawk-bobby-carpenter | access-date=2025-08-07}}</ref> In [[2003 Ohio State Buckeyes football team|2003]], Carpenter started three contests at [[Linebacker#Strongside linebacker|strongside linebacker]], totaling 37 tackles (24 solos), 4.5 sacks, 6.5 stops for losses and a pair of forced fumbles.

Carpenter was a full-time starter in [[2004 Ohio State Buckeyes football team|2004]], lining up at strongside linebacker. He finished second on the team with 93 tackles (46 solos) and registered two sacks with 6.5 stops behind the line of scrimmage. He also deflected three passes and intercepted three others.

As a senior in [[2005 Ohio State Buckeyes football team|2005]], Carpenter started first eleven games of the 2005 season, finishing fifth on the squad with 49 tackles and second on the team with eight sacks and 10.5 stops for losses, earning second-team All-Big Ten Conference honors. In the final game against Michigan, he fractured his right leg/ankle and was unable to play in the Fiesta Bowl.<ref name="p801">{{Cite web |last=Markey |first=Matt |date=2005-11-21 |title=Buckeyes' Laurinaitis handles initiation well |url=https://www.toledoblade.com/Ohio-State/2005/11/21/Buckeyes-Laurinaitis-handles-initiation-well.html |access-date=2024-12-27 |website=The Blade}}</ref>

===Dallas Cowboys===
Carpenter was the [[Dallas Cowboys]]' first round selection (18th overall) in the [[2006 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=2006 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2006/draft.htm |access-date=2023-05-09 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=2019-04-17|title=What happened to Bobby Carpenter? The best, worst linebacker draft picks in Cowboys history|url=https://www.dallasnews.com/sports/cowboys/2019/04/17/what-happened-to-bobby-carpenter-the-best-worst-linebacker-draft-picks-in-cowboys-history/|access-date=2020-07-27|website=Dallas News|language=en}}</ref> It was later reported that head coach [[Bill Parcells]] influenced the organization into drafting him, based on his previous experience coaching his father, [[Rob Carpenter (running back)|Rob Carpenter]]. His best game with the Cowboys came in a [[2006 NFL season|2006]] playoff loss to the [[Seattle Seahawks]], where he started at [[outside linebacker]] and recorded five tackles and three deflected passes.

In [[2009 NFL season|2009]], he took over the team's nickel [[linebacker]] role after playing mostly on [[special teams]]. Over his four-year stint with the Cowboys, Carpenter failed to establish a starting role, registering 96 tackles and 29 [[special teams]] tackles. In the fourth episode of the 2008 ''[[Hard Knocks (documentary series)|Hard Knocks]]'' series, Carpenter was continuously beaten in a pads and shorts practice by [[right tackle]] [[Marc Colombo]]. During that practice Colombo referred to him as "Barbie Carpenter", while also making fun of his shoulder length blonde hair.

===St. Louis Rams===
Carpenter was traded from the [[Dallas Cowboys]] to the [[St. Louis Rams]] in exchange for offensive tackle [[Alex Barron (American football)|Alex Barron]] on May 10, [[2010 NFL season|2010]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1986/06/14/sports/carpenter-is-traded-to-rams.html|title=Carpenter is Traded to Rams|work=The New York Times|date=14 June 1986 |access-date=23 August 2015|last1=Thomas Jr. |first1=Robert Mcg. }}</ref> He was cut before the start of the season on September 4.<ref>{{cite web | title=Rams give up on "Barbie" Carpenter, others | website=NBC Sports | date=2010-09-04 | url=https://www.nbcsports.com/nfl/profootballtalk/rumor-mill/news/rams-give-up-on-barbie-carpenter-others | access-date=2025-08-02}}</ref>

===Miami Dolphins===
On September 6, [[2010 NFL season|2010]], the [[Miami Dolphins]] signed Carpenter as a free agent, reuniting him with [[Bill Parcells]], who drafted him with the [[Dallas Cowboys]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=Nelson|first=Chris J.|title=Miami Dolphins Sign Former Dallas Cowboys Linebacker Bobby Carpenter|url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/453015-miami-dolphins-sign-former-dallas-cowboys-linebacker-bobby-carpenter|access-date=2020-07-27|website=Bleacher Report|language=en}}</ref> He was waived on October 18, because of a mistake on his [[special teams]] blocking assignment against the [[2010 Green Bay Packers season|Green Bay Packers]], that came on the heels of two previous blocking assignment errors against the [[2010 New England Patriots season|New England Patriots]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sun-sentinel.com/sports/fl-xpm-2010-10-18-sfl-dolphins-release-bobby-carpenter-101810-story.html|title=Miami Dolphins release Bobby Carpenter after special teams gaffe|work=tribunedigital-sunsentinel|date=October 18, 2010|access-date=23 August 2015}}</ref>

===Detroit Lions===
Carpenter was signed as a free agent by the [[Detroit Lions]] on October 20, [[2010 NFL season|2010]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kowalski |first=Tom  |date=October 21, 2010 |title=Detroit Lions' signings of Bobby Carpenter, Cody Wallace have a twist |url=https://www.mlive.com/lions/2010/10/detroit_lions_signings_of_carp.html |access-date=23 August 2015 |website=MLive.com}}</ref> Following the signings of [[Justin Durant]] and [[Stephen Tulloch]], it looked like Carpenter would test free agency again, but he was re-signed after the injury and release of [[Zack Follett]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=Schottey|first=Michael|title=Detroit Lions: Bobby Carpenter Likely Headed Elsewhere After Linebacker Signings|url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/787862-detroit-lions-bobby-carpenter-likely-headed-elsewhere-after-linebacker-signings|access-date=2020-07-27|website=Bleacher Report|language=en}}</ref>

On October 2, [[2011 NFL season|2011]], Carpenter had six tackles, a pass deflected and made the play of the game, returning an interception for a [[touchdown]], which sparked a second half come-from-behind victory against his former team, the [[2010 Dallas Cowboys season|Dallas Cowboys]]. The 24-point collapse was Dallas' largest blown lead in team history and eventually cost them a chance to qualify for the post-season.<ref>{{cite web|last=Wywrot|first=Chrissie|title=Lions beat Cowboys 34-30 in come-from-behind fashion|url=http://www.detroitlions.com/news/article-1/Lions-beat-Cowboys-34-30-in-come-from-behind-fashion/961eb5ac-2667-4a4e-b012-99ce46744b86|work=Detroit Lions Official Website|access-date=1 November 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111105020121/http://www.detroitlions.com/news/article-1/Lions-beat-Cowboys-34-30-in-come-from-behind-fashion/961eb5ac-2667-4a4e-b012-99ce46744b86|archive-date=5 November 2011|url-status=dead}}</ref>

===New England Patriots===
On April 5, 2012, Carpenter was signed as a free agent by the [[New England Patriots]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=October 30, 2012 |title=Patriots release LB Bobby Carpenter |url=https://www.patriots.com/news/patriots-release-lb-bobby-carpenter-183676?campaign=sf:fanshare:facebook |access-date=2020-07-27 |website=Patriots.com |language=en-US}}</ref> He was among the team's final pre-season cuts on September 1. After fellow linebacker [[Dont'a Hightower]] suffered a hamstring injury, the Patriots re-signed Carpenter on October 3.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.csnne.com/football-new-england-patriots/patriots-talk/Source-Bobby-Carpenter-set-to-return-to-?blockID=782935&feedID=10426|archive-url=https://archive.today/20130120041143/http://www.csnne.com/football-new-england-patriots/patriots-talk/Source-Bobby-Carpenter-set-to-return-to-?blockID=782935&feedID=10426|url-status=dead|archive-date=20 January 2013|title=Source: Bobby Carpenter set to return to Patriots|work=Comcast SportsNet - CSNNE.com|access-date=23 August 2015}}</ref> He was released on October 31 after playing in four games for New England, mostly on [[special teams]] while registering two special teams tackles.

== Media career==
In 2013, Carpenter joined 97.1 The Fan [[WBNS-FM]] in Columbus, Ohio and currently serves as a co-host on the morning show, Morning Juice, airing from 6am - 9am. During that time he also appear on Wall to Wall Sports for WBNS 10TV, which was also owned by Dispatch Media Group now owned by [[Tegna Inc.]] Carpenter has worked the Ohio State Spring game since 2016 for BTN and has been a color analyst for ESPN 3 since 2017.

In 2018, Carpenter became a regular contributor to ESPN's ''[[Get Up (TV program)|Get Up]]'', which airs daily from 8 AM to 10 AM EST.

In 2021, Carpenter began making appearances on ''[[The Pat McAfee Show]]''. He is jokingly referred to as "General Bob", due to his "rallying of the troops" which led to the [[Big Ten Conference]] reversing their decision to suspend the [[2020 Big Ten Conference football season|2020 season]].<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://www.si.com/college/michigan/football/michigan-football-2020-season-fall-big-ten-kevin-warren-bobby-carpenter-jim-harbaugh|title=ESPN Analyst Bobby Carpenter Helped Rally Michigan Troops|magazine=Sports Illustrated|first=Eric|last=Rutter|date=September 17, 2020|access-date=October 27, 2023}}</ref> In 2023, he has a recurring college football segment, in which he ranks the top five football programs of the past weekend.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2_YAKzY6oJs|title=The Pat McAfee Show {{!}} Wednesday August 30th, 2023|date=August 30, 2023|via=YouTube}}</ref> It has since become a running joke that he always picks his [[Home (sports)#Homerism|alma mater, Ohio State, as number one]].

==Personal life==
Carpenter is the son of former [[Houston Oilers]], [[New York Giants]] and [[Los Angeles Rams]] [[running back]] [[Rob Carpenter (running back)|Rob Carpenter]].<ref>{{cite web | last=Gutridge | first=Matt | title=Buckeye Pipelines: Lancaster Legends Rex Kern, Bobby Carpenter and Jim Cordle Made Their Mark at Ohio State | website=Eleven Warriors | date=2022-05-28 | url=https://www.elevenwarriors.com/ohio-state-football/2022/05/131042/buckeye-pipelines-lancaster-legends-rex-kern-bobby-carpenter-and-jim-cordle-made-their-mark-at-ohio-state | access-date=2025-08-07}}</ref> Carpenter and his father both played for [[Bill Parcells]]. He has three younger brothers: Jonathan, Georgie and Nathan. Carpenter is married to his wife Cortney, with whom he has four children.<ref name="Agonis" />

After completing his NFL career in 2013, Carpenter returned to Ohio State and completed his MBA with a specialization in Finance and Strategy. He is now an adjunct professor teaching a course at the [[Fisher College of Business]] in Private Equity.

Carpenter is currently a board member of the 2nd and Seven Foundation, which promotes literacy to second graders throughout [[Columbus, Ohio]], and the nation, and heavily involved with the Buckeye Cruise for Cancer that has raised over $20 million for the James Cancer Hospital since 2008.

In April 2022, Carpenter opened Carpenter Heating, Cooling, Plumbing, and  Electric in Columbus with co-owner Jeff Fry. He said it is a division of Freeland Contracting, which does large commercial jobs. Carpenter's company will focus on residential clients in central Ohio.{{Citation needed|date=July 2022}}

'''Bobby Joe Edmonds Jr.''' (born September 26, 1964) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Seattle Seahawks]], [[Los Angeles Raiders]], and [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] from 1986 to 1989 and 1995. Edmonds played [[college football]] for the [[Arkansas Razorbacks football|Arkansas Razorbacks]] and was selected by Seattle in the fifth round of the [[1986 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1986 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1986/draft.htm |access-date=2023-10-02 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref name="MoyerWyman2008">{{cite book|last1=Moyer|first1=Paul|last2=Wyman|first2=Dave|last3=Cluff|first3=Chris|title="Then Zorn Said to Largent...": The Best Seattle Seahawks Stories Ever Told|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SxgsDAAAQBAJ&pg=PT106|accessdate=26 December 2017|year=2008|publisher=Triumph Books|isbn=9781617492075|page=106}}</ref> Edmonds still holds two Seahawks records, most [[punt return]] yards gained in a career (1,010 yards) and most punt return yards gained in a season (419 yards).  He also made the AFC [[Pro Bowl]] squad in 1986 as a [[rookie]].

A 1982 graduate of [[Lutheran High School North (Missouri)|Lutheran High School North]], in [[St. Louis, Missouri]], Edmonds had a successful college career in football as a running back at the University of Arkansas where he returned after his football career to complete a bachelor's degree in broadcasting. After working as an occasional sports writer and color commentator, Edmonds has opened a gallery for fine art.

Edmonds at one time hosted his own show "The Lunch Special" on the Hog Sports Radio Network in Northwest Arkansas. He has two sons.

'''Robert Louis Tucker''' (born June 8, 1945) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[tight end]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL).  A 6'3", 230 lb. tight end from [[Bloomsburg University of Pennsylvania|Bloomsburg State College]], Tucker played for 11 seasons in the NFL, from 1970 to 1977 for the [[New York Giants]] and 1977 to 1980 for the [[Minnesota Vikings]].

In 1971 Tucker became the first NFL tight end to lead the league in receptions, topping the NFC with 59 catches for the Giants.<ref name=lcshof>[https://www.luzernecountysportshalloffame.com/portfolio_page/robert-tucker/ Robert Tucker], Luzerne County Sports Hall of Fame</ref>

Prior to joining the NFL, Tucker lettered in football and basketball at Hazleton High. At Bloomsburg State College, Tucker set three NAIA pass receiving records and went on to establish league records with the Pottstown the [[Pottstown Firebirds]],<ref name=lcshof/> whom he played for in the [[Atlantic Coast Football League]], along with the Lowell Giants.<ref name=drken119>Dr. Ken (September 2013). [http://www.helmethut.com/Features/Dr.Ken119.html ONE DEFINITION OF "MINOR LEAGUE" FOOTBALL, PART TWO] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304051058/http://www.helmethut.com/Features/Dr.Ken119.html |date=March 4, 2016 }}. ''HelmetHut.com''. Retrieved September 10, 2015.</ref> In 1969, He was a member of the Philadelphia Eagles taxi squad in 1969, and signed in 1970 as a free agent with the New York Giants.<ref name=lcshof/>

Tucker is one of the few Giants to play for the team in four different home stadiums: [[Yankee Stadium (1923)|Yankee Stadium]] (1970 through the first two home games of 1973); the [[Yale Bowl]] (last five home games of 1973 and all of 1974); [[Shea Stadium]] (1975) and [[Giants Stadium]] (1976–77).  He lived in [[Lincroft, New Jersey|Lincroft]], a neighborhood in [[Middletown Township, New Jersey]].<ref>Harvin, Al. [https://www.nytimes.com/1973/01/12/archives/an-offseason-game-new-jersey-sports.html "An Offseason Game; New Jersey Sports"], ''[[The New York Times]]'', January 12, 1973. Accessed November 16, 2008. "Some of the other Jersey residents on the team, according to Davis, are Bob Tucker, the New York Giants' tight end from Lincroft; Phil Villapiano, Oakland Raider linebacker from Ocean Township, and Ron Johnson, Giant running back, now a resident of Fort Lee."</ref>

Tucker was inducted into the American Football Association's Semi Pro Football Hall of Fame in 1982.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.americanfootballassn.com/forms/2010HallofFameListing.pdf |title=AFA Hall of Fame Class of 2020 |access-date=August 29, 2011 |archive-date=January 22, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160122083011/http://www.americanfootballassn.com/forms/2010HallofFameListing.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Tucker was a biology teacher and freshman football coach at [[Acton-Boxborough Regional High School]] in [[Acton, Massachusetts]] in 1969.<ref>"The 1969 Torch" Year Book for Acton Boxboro Regional High School</ref>

By the time he walked into training camp that season, he had gained 50 pounds that shocked his coaches.{{Cite web |title=ESPNMAG.com - Big Night |url=https://www.espn.com/magazine/vol6no03strongmen.html |access-date=2025-01-17 |website=www.espn.com}} It soon spread to having other Cardinal [[Lineman (gridiron football)#Offensive line|offensive linemen]] work on their physique with modern [[Powerlifting|weightlifting]]/[[powerlifting]] that eventually became a league obsession. That season, the offensive line quintet of tackles [[Roger Finnie]] & [[Dan Dierdorf]], center [[Tom Banks (American football)|Tom Banks]], and guards in [[Conrad Dobler]] and Young allowed just eight sacks in the entire fourteen-game season (the next time the Cardinals had three games with no sacks taken would not come until 2024).{{Cite web |title=The Historical - And Current - Context Of Sack-Less Protection Streak |url=https://www.azcardinals.com/news/cardinals-historical-and-current-context-of-sack-less-protection-streak |access-date=2025-01-17 |website=www.azcardinals.com |language=en-US}} Young was named to two [[Pro Bowl|Pro Bowls]] ([[1979 Pro Bowl|1978]] & [[1980 Pro Bowl|1979]]) and was a first-team [[All-Pro]] selection in 1979 as well. A hit he suffered in the Pro Bowl in 1979 would soon hasten the end of his career, as St. Louis cut him at the end of the 1979 season. Years later, Young admitted to his wife that he never felt any better than when he was on steroids. Young freely admitted to his use of steroids in his playing career, stating that he used it lightly in college before eventually using them for eight seasons when his brother convinced him about steroids being safe in moderation, which he would use in his later days in St. Louis and in Houston. He played just two games in 1981 for the Saints and retired.{{Cite web |last=Domowitch |first=Paul |date=2009-06-01 |title=Steroids' effects: Harmless or a killer? |url=https://www.inquirer.com/philly/news/special_packages/dailynews/Steroids_effects_Harmless_or_a_killer.html |access-date=2025-01-17 |website= |language=en}}{{Cite web |last=SteelersFan |first=Tim |title=The Steelers, Steroids, and Profound Misconceptions |url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/232404-the-steelers-steroids-and-profound-misconceptions |access-date=2025-01-17 |website=Bleacher Report |language=en}} In 1986, he was inducted into the [[Howard Payne University]] Sports Hall of Fame for his playing career in football along with track and field.{{cite web | url=https://hpusports.com/hof.aspx?hof=10 | title=Robert A. "Bob" Young (1986) - HPU Sports Hall of Fame }} ==Power lifting== He was the older brother of three-time world powerlifting champion [[Doug Young (powerlifter)|Doug Young]].{{Cite web |url=http://stlsportshistory.com/blog2/2010/08/03/remember-bob-young/ |title=Remember Bob Young|website=stlsportshistory.com |access-date=2013-01-06 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120717044831/http://stlsportshistory.com/blog2/2010/08/03/remember-bob-young/ |archive-date=2012-07-17 |url-status=dead }} Young competed in the inaugural [[World's Strongest Man]] contest in 1977, finishing second to weightlifter [[Bruce Wilhelm]]. He also finished 5th in the [[1979 World's Strongest Man]]. ==Coaching career== After his pro career, Young coached in the USFL from 1982 to 1986 as an offensive line coach for the [[Houston Gamblers]]. He coached the offensive line at [[University of Houston]] from 1987 to 1989, and for the [[Houston Oilers]] from 1990 to 1995. ==Death== Young was married three times. After his career ended, he maintained a smoking habit and was considered obese to go along with having [[diabetes]]. '''Robert Conrad Anderson''' (born October 11, 1947) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Halfback (American football)|halfback]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for five seasons during the 1970s. He played [[college football]] for the [[Colorado Buffaloes football|Colorado Buffaloes]], earning consensus [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] honors in 1969. He was selected in the first round of the [[1970 NFL draft]], and played in the league for the [[Denver Broncos]], [[New England Patriots]] and [[Washington Commanders|Washington Redskins]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). Anderson was inducted into the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] in 2006.

== Early life ==

Anderson was born in [[Midland, Michigan]].  He attended [[Boulder High School]] in [[Boulder, Colorado]]; following his senior season at Boulder he won the Gold Helmet award for being Colorado's top football player.

== College career ==

Anderson attended the [[University of Colorado Boulder]], where he played for the [[Colorado Buffaloes football|Buffaloes]] from 1967 to 1969.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.buffzone.com/2020/09/19/looking-back-bobby-andersons-stellar-cu-buffs-debut/ | title=Looking back: Bobby Anderson's stellar CU Buffs debut | date=19 September 2020 }}</ref> He was the Buffaloes' dual-threat running quarterback during his sophomore and junior seasons, and led the team in both rushing and passing. The 1967 Buffaloes finished 9–2 and second in the [[Big Eight Conference]], and Anderson scored twice as Colorado beat the [[Miami Hurricanes football|Miami Hurricanes]] in the Bluebonnet Bowl. The 1968 Buffaloes finished 8–3, for third in the conference. When the 1969 Buffaloes faced injuries in the backfield, Anderson shifted to running back for the third game. The team finished third in the conference and went to the Liberty Bowl, where he rushed for a bowl record 254 yards and three touchdowns in a 47–33 victory over the [[1969 Alabama Crimson Tide football team|Alabama Crimson Tide]]. Following his senior season, Anderson was recognized as a consensus first-team All-American.

Anderson's older brother [[Dick Anderson|Dick]] played for Colorado as a defensive back from 1965 to 1967.

== Professional career ==

The Denver Broncos selected Anderson in the first round (11th pick overall) of the 1970 NFL Draft, and he played for the Broncos from {{NFL Year|1970}} to {{NFL Year|1973}}.  He played a final NFL season in {{NFL Year|1975}}, splitting the year between the New England Patriots and Washington Redskins.  In five NFL seasons, Anderson played in fifty-three games, and rushed 313 times for 1,282 yards and nine touchdowns.  He also had eighty-four receptions for 861 yards and two touchdowns.

== Post-playing career ==
Anderson formerly served as a long-time broadcaster on the CU Football Network. Anderson also appeared in the 1977 Robbie Benson movie ''[[One on One (1977 film)|One on One]]'' as "Hitman King", as well as in the 1985 [[Kevin Costner]] bicycling film "American Flyers" as a reporter.

'''Bobby Lee Johnson''' (born December 14, 1961) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[wide receiver]] for three seasons with the [[New York Giants]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL).  He played [[college football]] for the [[Kansas Jayhawks football|Kansas Jayhawks]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.nfl.com/players/bobby-johnson/ |title=Bobby Johnson |publisher=NFL |access-date=2022-06-09}}</ref>

He is best known as the receiver who caught [[Phil Simms]]' 4th and 17 pass in Minnesota in week 12 of the 1986 season.  It is the play that many football historians feel turned the tide of the Giants championship run.  The play set up Raul Allegre's game winning 33-yard field goal.  The Giants won the game 22 - 20.

Following the 1986 NFL season, Johnson was traded to the San Diego Chargers. He was routinely late to practice as a result of his blossoming crack cocaine addiction and was subsequently cut two weeks later. In 1989, after years of homelessness and addiction, Johnson sold his Super Bowl XXI ring at a pawn shop in Nashville, TN for $250. Johnson has been clean since 2002. In 2016, Lee Einsidler, a sports fan, led the charge to reunite Johnson with his ring. Enlisting the help of Johnson's former head coach, Bill Parcells, Einsidler was successful in doing so.<ref>{{cite web| url = https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/18046804/nfl-2016-new-york-giants-wr-bobby-johnson-got-super-bowl-ring-back-pawning-drugs| title = NFL 2016 - New York Giants WR Bobby Johnson got his Super Bowl ring back after pawning it for drugs| date = 15 November 2016}}</ref>

'''Robert Charles Jackson''' (born December 23, 1956) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[cornerback]] for the [[New York Jets]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He retired with 21 career interceptions and 3 fumble recoveries.

==College==
Jackson started at Florida State University and in 1993 was inducted into the FSU Hall of Fame.<ref>[https://archive.today/20121214173231/http://varsityclub.fsu.edu/community/Page.aspx?pid=1825 Varsity Club - 1993 Bios - Florida State University]</ref>
 
Jackson once held the all time interception record at FSU, since broken by [[Terrell Buckley]]. Jackson also held the single game-punt return average of 45.3 yard per return (minimum three returns) -- a record since broken by Jet star [[Leon Washington]].

==Professional career==
His professional career began when he was selected in the sixth round of the National Football League draft of 1978.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1978 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1978/draft.htm |access-date=2024-03-17 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He went on to start all 16 games at cornerback his rookie year. He also tied for the team lead with 5 interceptions and was named to the “AFC All-Rookie Team” as a starter.

He played [[college football]] for the [[Utah State Aggies football|Utah State Aggies]] and was selected in the eighth round of the [[1972 NFL draft|1972 National Football League (NFL) draft]] by the [[St. Louis Cardinals (NFL)|St. Louis Cardinals]]. He played in the NFL as a [[wide receiver]] for two seasons, appearing for the Cardinals, [[Green Bay Packers]] and [[New Orleans Saints]]. ==Early life== Wicks was born on July 24, 1950, in [[Pasadena, California]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/W/WickBo20.htm|website=[[Pro Football Reference]]|access-date=June 7, 2025|title=Bob Wicks Stats}} He grew up competing in [[American football|football]], [[baseball]], [[basketball]], and [[track and field]].{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-herald-journal/174056075/|newspaper=[[The Herald Journal]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=September 16, 1971|title=Utah State's Pseudo Twins|page=13|author=Mitchell, Ken}} {{Open access}} Starting in [[fourth grade]] and continuing through college, he was often teammates with [[quarterback]] [[John Strycula]], who lived nearby. Wicks attended [[Royal Oak High School (California)|Royal Oak High School]] in [[Covina, California]], along with Strycula, where he played [[American football|football]] as an [[End (gridiron football)|end]] and [[Safety (gridiron football position)|safety]].{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-daily-report/174054535/|newspaper=[[The Daily Report (Ontario, California)|The Daily Report]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=November 25, 1967|page=5|title=Romo, Aleman Gain Dual All-Loop Honors}} {{Open access}} He was the first Royal Oak alumnus to play in the [[National Football League|NFL]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/schools/high_schools.cgi?id=93c0b599|website=[[Pro Football Reference]]|access-date=June 7, 2025|title=Royal Oak (Covina, CA) Alumni Pro Stats}} He was All-[[Hacienda League]] as a [[Junior (education year)|junior]] and as a [[Senior (education)|senior]] in 1967, he was named first-team all-league at both end and safety. In addition to football, he was also an all-league performer in basketball at Royal Oak. Wicks accepted a [[Athletic scholarship|scholarship]] to play [[college football]] for the [[Utah State Aggies football|Utah State Aggies]], where he was joined by Strycula.{{Cite news|url=https://sunlakessplash.com/softball-player-profile-bob-wicks/|newspaper=[[Sun Lake Splash]]|title=Softball Player Profile: Bob Wicks|author=Wolfe, Larry|date=February 1, 2019}} ==College career== With the [[freshman]] team in 1968 at Utah State, Wicks played "anything and anywhere".{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/student-life/174057259/|newspaper=[[Student Life (Utah State)|Student Life]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=November 23, 1970|page=7|title=Wicks blazing All-American path|author=Hansen, Greg}} {{Open access}} In addition to playing [[defensive back]] and as a backup [[Tailback (American football)|tailback]], he was also used as a [[return specialist]], recording a 70-yard [[Punt (gridiron football)|punt]] return [[touchdown]] against [[Snow College]]. He debuted for the [[varsity team]] in 1969 against [[Wichita State Shockers football|Wichita State]] but suffered an injury that limited him for the rest of the season. Nevertheless, he was a starter at [[wide receiver]] and caught 19 passes for 272 yards, scoring two touchdowns in the season finale. In 1970, Wicks helped Utah State compile a record of 5–5 while being among the nation's leading receivers and punt returners.{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-herald-journal/174058349/|newspaper=[[The Herald Journal]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=December 2, 1970|page=10|title=Aggies Set Several New Records}} {{Open access}} He caught 47 passes for 642 yards and had 16 punt returns for 279 yards and two touchdowns, averaging 17.4 yards per return. He then caught a team-leading 58 passes for 862 yards as a senior while Utah State compiled a record of 8–3. That year, he set the Utah State single-season record with 58 receptions, set the career record with 124 total receptions, and tied the school's single-game receptions record (13) while setting the single-game receiving yards record (211) against [[Idaho Vandals football|Idaho]].{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-herald-journal/174059716/|newspaper=[[The Herald Journal]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=December 9, 1971|page=6|title=Bob Wicks Invited To Play In Senior Bowl}} {{Open access}} He scored a total of 10 touchdowns at Utah State and was invited to the [[Senior Bowl]] at the conclusion of his collegiate career. ==Professional career== Wicks was selected by the [[St. Louis Cardinals (NFL)|St. Louis Cardinals]] in the eighth round (188th overall) of the [[1972 NFL draft]].{{Cite web|url=https://profootballarchives.com/players/w/wick00800.html|website=Pro Football Archives|access-date=June 7, 2025|title=Bob Wicks Stats}} He signed his [[rookie]] contract in May 1972 and ended up making the team's final roster.{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-herald-journal/174059878/|newspaper=[[The Herald Journal]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=May 7, 1972|page=9|title=Bob Wicks Signs With Cardinals}} {{Open access}}{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/deseret-news/174059947/|newspaper=[[Deseret News]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=September 13, 1972|page=68|title=Cards Keep Ex-Ag Wicks}} {{Open access}} Wicks made his NFL debut in the Cardinals' Week 1 win over the [[Baltimore Colts]] and appeared in the team's first nine games, recording one catch for eight yards.{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/W/WickBo20/gamelog/|website=[[Pro Football Reference]]|access-date=June 8, 2025|title=Bob Wicks Career Game Log}} Following Week 9, he was sent to the Cardinals' [[Practice squad|taxi squad]].{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/st-louis-post-dispatch/174099709/|newspaper=[[St. Louis Post-Dispatch]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=November 19, 1972|page=40|title=Hutchison Activated; 2000 Tickets On Sale}} {{Open access}} He was released by the Cardinals on September 5, 1973.{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-herald-journal/174099924/|newspaper=[[The Herald Journal]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=September 6, 1973|page=11|title=Sports Briefing}} {{Open access}} On October 31, 1973, he signed with the [[San Diego Chargers]], though he was later released without playing in a game.{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/deseret-news/174100129/|newspaper=[[Deseret News]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=November 1, 1973|page=65|title=Ex-Ag Wicks signs with San Diego|agency=[[United Press International]]}} {{Open access}}{{Cite web|url=https://profootballarchives.com/transactions/w/wick00800.html|website=Pro Football Archives|access-date=June 8, 2025|title=Bob Wicks Transactions}} In 1974, Wicks signed with the [[Green Bay Packers]]. He made the final roster and appeared in the team's Week 1 loss to the [[Minnesota Vikings]]. He was mainly used on [[special teams]] for the Packers and then was released soon after his only game with the team.{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-herald-journal/174100624/|newspaper=[[The Herald Journal]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=October 1, 1974|page=7|title=Wicks Cut}} {{Open access}} In November, he signed with the [[New Orleans Saints]].{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-herald-journal/174100724/|newspaper=[[The Herald Journal]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=November 19, 1974|page=6|title=Ex-Aggie Wicks Inked In NFL}} {{Open access}} He played for the Saints in the final five games of the season on special teams.{{Cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/mexico-ledger/174100927/|newspaper=[[Mexico Ledger]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=July 9, 1975|page=14|title=Sports Shorts}} {{Open access}} He announced his retirement from professional football in July 1975, finishing his career with 15 games played and one reception for eight yards. ==Later life== With his wife, Kitty, Wicks has three sons and a daughter. Following his football career, he worked in Covina for a bus company before joining All Pack Company, Inc., a packaging business owned by his wife's parents. He worked for the business until his retirement and moved to Arizona in 2015. '''Robert Michael Howfield''' (born 3 December 1936) is an English former professional sportsman who played both [[association football]] and [[American football]].<ref name="Jones">{{cite book |last=Jones |first=Trefor |title=The Watford Football Club Illustrated Who's Who |publisher=T.G Jones |location=Surrey |year=1996|pages=125|isbn=0-9527458-0-1}}</ref>

==Early and personal life==
Howfield was born in [[Watford]]. His son [[Ian Howfield]] kicked for the [[Houston Oilers]] in 1991.

==Career==

===Association football===
Howfield played as a [[Forward (association football)|forward]], known for his volatility.<ref name="Jones"/> Howfield began his association football career with local side Bushey F.C., before signing amateur terms with [[Millwall F.C.|Millwall]] in May 1957.<ref name="Jones"/> He became a professional with [[Watford F.C.|Watford]] in September 1957, playing for the club until July 1959, when he moved to [[Crewe Alexandra F.C.|Crewe Alexandra]].<ref name="Jones"/> In October 1959, however, he moved to [[Aldershot F.C.|Aldershot]], where his 23 league goals in the [[1961-62 in English football|1961–62]] season were a club record for a number of years.<ref name="Jones"/> He played for the club until July 1962 when he returned to Watford for a "substantial fee".<ref name="Jones"/>

Howfield moved to [[Fulham F.C.|Fulham]] in November 1965 for £6000, having made 101 appearances and scored 25 goals in his two spells with the club.<ref name="Jones"/> He scored three goals for Fulham in the last ten goal performance by a top-flight club.<ref name="Jones"/>

During 1965 Howfield went to play with the [[New York Americans (soccer)|New York Americans]] of the [[International Soccer League (1960-1965)|International Soccer League]].<ref name="Jones"/> He returned to Aldershot in August 1965, playing for the [[Hampshire]] club until 1967,<ref name="Jones"/> before playing non-League football with [[Chelmsford City F.C.|Chelmsford City]].<ref>[http://www.neilbrown.newcastlefans.com/player/bobbyhowfield.html Post War English & Scottish Football League A - Z Player's Transfer Database]</ref>

===American football===
Known for his powerful kicks,<ref name="Jones"/> Howfield returned to America to take up American football as a placekicker. Between 1968 and 1970 he played for the [[Denver Broncos]]. Following the 1970 season, the Broncos traded Howfield to the [[New York Jets]] for [[Jim Turner (placekicker)|Jim Turner]].<ref name=howfield>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1971/01/28/archives/jets-send-turner-to-broncos-for-howfield-in-deal-for-kicking.html |title=Jets Send Turner to Broncos for Howfield in Deal for Kicking Specialists - The New York Times |publisher=Nytimes.com |date=28 January 1971 |accessdate=13 June 2023}}</ref> He played for the Jets until 1974.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nfl.com/players/bobby-howfield/|title=Bobby Howfield Stats, News and Video - K|website=NFL.com}}</ref>

==Later life==
After his retirement from sport, Howfield worked in the insurance department of a Denver bank, and he still lives close to the city.<ref>[http://www.wfc.net/watn.htm Where are they now?], wfc.net</ref><!--Source reliable?-->

'''Robert Lindsay Greenwood Jr.''' (born March 2, 1987), commonly known as '''Bobby Greenwood''', is a former [[defensive end]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He was signed by the Chiefs as an [[undrafted free agent]] in 2009. He played [[college football]] at [[Alabama Crimson Tide football|Alabama]].

At Alabama, Greenwood was a solid contributor on defense for all four seasons. In 2005, he was named to the 2005 All-SEC Freshman Team. Against [[Auburn Tigers football|Auburn]] in 2008, he blocked a field goal attempt to preserve a 10–0 Crimson Tide lead at the half. The Tide would go on to win 36–0.

'''Bobby Felder''' (born September 23, 1990) is an American former professional [[Gridiron football|football]] [[cornerback]]. He signed with the Vikings after going undrafted in the [[2012 NFL draft]].

==Early life==
Felder attended [[McComb High School]] in [[McComb, Mississippi]].

==College career==
Felder enrolled at [[Nicholls State Colonels football|Nicholls State University]] after receiving scholarship offers from at least two other schools.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://recruiting.scout.com/2/724617.html |title=Scout.com: Mid-Week Visit Could Seal the Deal |website=recruiting.scout.com |access-date=22 May 2022 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130201214313/http://recruiting.scout.com/2/724617.html |archive-date=1 February 2013 |url-status=dead}}</ref>  He cited fellow NFL cornerback and [[Nicholls State Colonels football|Nicholls State]] alum [[Ladarius Webb]] as one of the reasons for choosing [[Nicholls State Colonels football|Nicholls State]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.dailynorseman.com/2012/8/1/3212687/bobby-felder-makes-an-impact|title = Bobby Felder Makes an Impact|date = August 2012}}</ref>

Felder had 11 career interceptions in college.

==Professional career==
Felder went undrafted and subsequently signed with the Minnesota Vikings on May 1, 2012.  He was waived by the team on August 31, 2012, and signed to the Vikings practice squad the next day.  After re-signing with the team on January 7, 2013, Felder was put on the injured reserve list of the Minnesota Vikings on August 31, 2013, as the team trimmed its players to a 53-man roster.<ref>{{cite news |first=Arif |last=Hasan |title=Minnesota Vikings Release Final 53-Man Roster, Final Cuts |url=http://www.dailynorseman.com/2013/8/31/4681032/minnesota-vikings-release-final-53-man-roster-final-cuts |work=DailyNorseman.com |publisher=SB Nation |date=August 31, 2013 |accessdate=September 1, 2013 }}</ref>

Tampa Bay Buccaneers claimed Bobby Felder off waivers from the Vikings on October 29, 2013.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.buccaneers.com/news/article-smith/Bucs-Grab-CB-Felder-Off-Waivers/76553c6c-c4dc-4762-9e6f-ca2c4da27648 |title=Bucs Grab CB Felder off Waivers |access-date=October 30, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131101203022/http://www.buccaneers.com/news/article-smith/Bucs-Grab-CB-Felder-Off-Waivers/76553c6c-c4dc-4762-9e6f-ca2c4da27648 |archive-date=November 1, 2013 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

He was signed by the [[Buffalo Bills]] but waived on Sept 3rd, 2014.

On January 12, 2016, Felder was assigned to the [[Orlando Predators]] of the [[Arena Football League]] (AFL).<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.oursportscentral.com/services/releases/orlando-predators-add-former-nfl-db-bobby-felder/n-5088871 |title=Orlando Predators Add Former NFL DB Bobby Felder |date=January 12, 2016 |publisher=OurSports Central |work=www.oursportscentral.com |accessdate=January 12, 2016}}</ref> On March 22, 2016, Felder was placed on recallable reassignment.

'''Bobby Daniel Brooks''' (born February 24, 1951) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[cornerback]] for three seasons with the [[New York Giants]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He was selected by the Giants in the 11th round of the [[1974 NFL draft]] after playing [[college football]] for the [[Bishop Tigers football|Bishop Tigers]].

==Early life and college==
Bobby Daniel Brooks was born on February 24, 1951, in [[Dallas, Texas]].<ref name="pfa">{{cite web | url=https://www.profootballarchives.com/players/b/broo01200.html | title=BOBBY BROOKS | publisher=profootballarchives.com | accessdate=27 December 2024}}</ref> He attended [[I.M. Terrell High School]] in [[Fort Worth, Texas]].<ref name="pfa"/>

He played [[college football]] for the [[Bishop Tigers football|Tigers]] of [[Bishop College]] from 1970 to 1973.<ref name="pfa"/>

==Professional career==
Brooks was selected by the [[New York Giants]] in the 11th round, with the 263rd overall pick, of the [[1974 NFL draft]], and by the [[Memphis Southmen]] in the 21st round, with the 244th overall pick, of the [[1974 WFL draft]].<ref name="pfr">{{cite web | url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/B/BrooBo20.htm | title=Bobby Brooks | publisher=pro-football-reference.com | accessdate=27 December 2024}}</ref><ref name="pfa"/> He signed with the Giants in 1974.<ref name="transactions"/> Brooks played in all 14 games for the Giants during the 1974 season, returning five kicks for 106 yards and one punt for nine yards.<ref name="pfr"/> He started all 14 games at left [[cornerback]] the following year in 1975, recording four interceptions and one fumble recovery, as the Giants finished the season with a 5–9 record.<ref name="pfr"/><ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/nyg/1975.htm | title=1975 New York Giants | publisher=pro-football-reference.com | accessdate=27 December 2024}}</ref> He appeared in four games, all starts, during the 1976 season, totaling one interception and one fumble recovery.<ref name="pfr"/> He was released by the Giants on September 14, 1977.<ref name="transactions"/><ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.nytimes.com/1977/09/15/archives/giants-waive-bobby-brooks-sign-pietrzak-giants-place-brooks-colbert.html | title=Giants Waive Bobby Brooks, Sign Pietrzak | work=[[The New York Times]] | date=September 15, 1977 | accessdate=27 December 2024 | author=Katz, Michael}}</ref>

Brooks signed with the [[Denver Broncos]] on July 17, 1978.<ref name="transactions">{{cite web | url=https://www.profootballarchives.com/transactions/b/broo01200.html | title=Bobby Brooks NFL Transactions | publisher=profootballarchives.com | accessdate=27 December 2024}}</ref> He was released on August 1, 1978.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.prosportstransactions.com/football/Search/SearchResults.php?Player=Bobby+Brooks&Team=&BeginDate=&EndDate=&PlayerMovementChkBx=yes&submit=Search | title=Search Results | publisher=prosportstransactions.com | accessdate=27 December 2024}}</ref>

'''Braynard Ontawyn Brown''' (born March 26, 1977) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[wide receiver]] for one season with the [[Cleveland Browns]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Notre Dame Fighting Irish football|Notre Dame Fighting Irish]].

==Early life==
Braynard Ontawyn Brown was born March 26, 1977, in [[Fort Lauderdale, Florida]].<ref name="pfa"/> He attended [[St. Thomas Aquinas High School (Fort Lauderdale, Florida)|St. Thomas Aquinas High School]] in [[Fort Lauderdale, Florida]].<ref name="pfa"/>

==College career==
Brown was a member of the [[Notre Dame Fighting Irish football|Notre Dame Fighting Irish]] of the [[University of Notre Dame]] from 1995 to 1999.<ref name="pfa">{{cite web | url=https://www.profootballarchives.com/players/b/brow02350.html | title=BOBBY BROWN | publisher=profootballarchives.com | accessdate=27 December 2024}}</ref> He was [[redshirted]] in 1995.<ref name="pfa"/> He caught two passes for 84 yards in 1996, 45 passes for 543 yards and six touchdowns in 1997, 13 passes for 286 yards and one touchdown in 1998, and 36 passes for 608 yards and five touchdowns in 1999.<ref name="sr">{{cite web | url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/bobby-brown-2.html | title=Bobby Brown | publisher=sports-reference.com | accessdate=27 December 2024}}</ref> He also participated in track at Notre Dame.<ref name="sons">{{cite web | url=https://www.herloyalsons.com/blog/2013/01/31/where-are-they-now-bobby-brown/ | title=WHERE ARE THEY NOW? BOBBY BROWN | publisher=herloyalsons.com | date=January 31, 2013 | accessdate=27 December 2024}}</ref> He graduated with a triple major in government, sociology and computer application with a minor in African-American studies.<ref name="sons"/>

==Professional career==
After going undrafted in the [[2000 NFL draft]], Brown signed with the [[Green Bay Packers]] on April 20, 2000.<ref name="transactions"/> He was later released on August 27, 2000.<ref name="transactions"/>

Brown was signed to the practice squad of the [[Cleveland Browns]] on August 29, 2000.<ref name="transactions"/> He was promoted to the active roster on November 11 and played in six games for the Browns during the 2000 season, recording two receptions for 14 yards on seven targets.<ref name="transactions"/><ref name="pfr"/> He also posted one solo tackle.<ref name="pfr"/> He was released the next year on August 29, 2001.<ref name="transactions"/> Brown was later signed to the Browns' practice squad on December 12, 2001.<ref name="transactions"/> He became a free agent after the season.<ref name="transactions">{{cite web | url=https://www.profootballarchives.com/transactions/b/brow02350.html | title=Bobby Brown NFL Transactions | publisher=profootballarchives.com | accessdate=27 December 2024}}</ref>

==Personal life==
After his NFL career, Brown graduated from [[Notre Dame Law School]] with a [[Juris Doctor]] and from the [[Yale School of Management]] with a [[Master of Business Administration]].<ref name="sons"/> He has worked as a corporate attorney and in the financial services industry.<ref name="south"/><ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.gelaw.com/attorneys/brown-2 | title=Braynard (Bobby) Brown | publisher=gelaw.com | accessdate=27 December 2024}}</ref> He has also served as a Councilman for [[South Orange, New Jersey]].<ref name="south">{{cite web | url=https://www.southorange.org/831/Councilman-Bobby-Brown | title=Councilman Bobby Brown | publisher=southorange.org | accessdate=27 December 2024}}</ref>

Browns is a member of [[Omega Psi Phi]].<ref name="sons"/> His nephew, [[Cody Riggs]], also played in the NFL.<ref name="pfr">{{cite web | url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/B/BrowBo00.htm | title=Bobby Brown | publisher=pro-football-reference.com | accessdate=27 December 2024}}</ref>

===New York Giants===
Hart was drafted by the [[New York Giants]] in the seventh round, 226th overall, in the [[2015 NFL draft]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Giants draft Florida State OL Bobby Hart in Round 7|url=http://www.giants.com/news-and-blogs/article-1/Giants-draft-Florida-State-OL-Bobby-Hart-in-Round-7/fb897e2a-6230-4544-988b-f7a3d070da6c|author=Salomone, Dan|website=Giants.com|date=May 2, 2015|access-date=February 14, 2018|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180215084330/http://www.giants.com/news-and-blogs/article-1/Giants-draft-Florida-State-OL-Bobby-Hart-in-Round-7/fb897e2a-6230-4544-988b-f7a3d070da6c|archive-date=February 15, 2018}}</ref> When the Giants drafted Hart, they projected him as a [[offensive guard|guard]] in the NFL.<ref name=CBS>{{cite news |title=Giants 7th Round Pick: Florida State Offensive Tackle Bobby Hart|url=http://newyork.cbslocal.com/2015/05/02/giants-7th-round-pick-florida-state-offensive-tackle-bobby-hart/ |work=[[CBS Sports]] |date=May 2, 2015 |access-date=May 6, 2012}}</ref> To prepare for the switch, he worked out with former [[Pro Bowl]] center [[LeCharles Bentley]].<ref name=Nj/> Hart, though, stayed primarily at right tackle in 2015.

In 2016, Hart started 13 games at [[right tackle]].

Hart entered the 2017 season as the Giants' second right tackle. He played in 10 games with 7 starts in 2017. He was [[waived/injured]] by the Giants on December 30, 2017 with an ankle injury and was placed on [[injured reserve]] after refusing to play in the team's season finale.<ref>{{cite web|title=Roster Moves: OT Hart Waived/Injured, WR King to IR, Three promoted from practice squad|url=http://www.giants.com/news-and-blogs/article-1/Roster-Moves-OT-Hart-WaivedInjured-WR-King-to-IR-Three-promoted-from-practice-squad/1e179a3c-8e73-4491-b0a3-6a8624dac2bd|author=Eisen, Michael|website=Giants.com|date=December 30, 2017|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180101235259/http://www.giants.com/news-and-blogs/article-1/Roster-Moves-OT-Hart-WaivedInjured-WR-King-to-IR-Three-promoted-from-practice-squad/1e179a3c-8e73-4491-b0a3-6a8624dac2bd|archive-date=January 1, 2018}}</ref> On February 9, 2018, Hart was released by the Giants.<ref>{{cite web|title=Giants waive Bobby Hart from injured reserve|url=http://profootballtalk.nbcsports.com/2018/02/09/giants-waive-bobby-hart-from-injured-reserve/|author=Williams, Charean|website=ProFootballTalk.NBCSports.com|date=February 9, 2018}}</ref>

On March 11, 2019, Hart signed a three-year, $16.15 million contract extension with the Bengals.<ref>{{cite web|title=Bengals re-sign Bobby Hart to 3-year contract worth $21 million|url=https://www.cincyjungle.com/2019/3/11/18260584/bengals-bobby-contract-21-million-nfl-news|website=CincyJungle.com|publisher=[[SB Nation]]|date=March 11, 2019|access-date=October 17, 2020}}</ref>

Hart started all 16 games in 2019. In 2020, he played in 14 games, starting 13, and was ranked 35th of 52 offensive tackles by [[Pro Football Focus]].<ref name="BN Hart">{{Cite web |last=Skurski |first=Jay |date=2020-03-30 |title=Bills sign former Bengals right tackle Bobby Hart to a one-year contract |url=https://buffalonews.com/sports/bills/bills-sign-former-bengals-right-tackle-bobby-hart-to-a-one-year-contract/article_3dcc7e06-9193-11eb-abd4-0f40ab7ae8fa.html |access-date=2021-09-05 |website=The Buffalo News |language=en}}</ref>

I don't discriminate against anybody. I know that everyone thinks differently and I know that I have a platform that sometimes people can see things and take it a certain way and I'm definitely aware of that. As you mature and grow, I talked to the players, coaches and things like that."<ref name="BN Hart" />

'''Robert Arlen White ''' (born April 9, 1963) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Center (gridiron football)|center]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Dallas Cowboys]] and [[New England Patriots]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Rhode Island Rams football|Rhode Island Rams]].

==Early life==
White attended [[Lunenburg High School]], where he was a Watchusetts League All-star. He accepted a football scholarship from the [[University of Rhode Island]]. He started his first two seasons for the [[Rhode Island Rams football|Rams]] at [[Center (gridiron football)|center]]. He started at [[left tackle]] as a junior.

As a senior, he started at right tackle in an offense that featured [[quarterback]] Tom Ehrhardt, who led the nation in total offense, passing an average of 50 times a game, while scoring a total of 42 [[touchdown]]s. He was named a team captain and was a part of two [[Yankee Conference]] titles in his last 2 years.<ref>{{cite news| title=Rhode Island Welcomes Newest Hall of Fame Class | publisher=University of Rhode Island | date=January 26, 2011}}</ref>

In 2011, he was inducted into the Rhode Island Athletics Hall of Fame.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://gorhody.com/honors/hall-of-fame?type=alpha | title=University of Rhode Island Athletic Hall of Fame | access-date=April 21, 2023}}</ref>

==Professional career==
===New York Jets===
White was selected by the [[New York Jets]] in the seventh round (189th overall) of the [[1986 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1986 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1986/draft.htm |access-date=2023-10-03 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=April 30, 1986 |title=Jets pick players to help shore up their porous offensive line |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1982&dat=19860430&id=WwVHAAAAIBAJ&sjid=pzMNAAAAIBAJ&pg=1573,3258466 |access-date=April 21, 2023 |website=The Evening News|agency=Associated Press|via=Google News}}</ref> He was waived on August 25.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1982&dat=19860826&id=Zb5GAAAAIBAJ&sjid=RDMNAAAAIBAJ&pg=4686,2640668 | title=Jets cut 2nd round draft pick | access-date=April 21, 2022}}</ref>

===Dallas Cowboys===
In [[1987 NFL season|1987]], he was signed as a [[free agent]] by the [[Dallas Cowboys]]. He began [[Training camp (National Football League)|training camp]] playing at [[offensive guard|guard]] and was switched to [[Center (gridiron football)|center]] for the last 2 weeks. He was released before the start of the season on September 7.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=110&dat=19870908&id=UsNRAAAAIBAJ&sjid=0lUDAAAAIBAJ&pg=1885,493176 | title=Transactions | access-date=April 21, 2023}}</ref> After the players went on a strike on the third week of the season, those games were canceled (reducing the 16-game season to 15) and the [[NFL]] decided that the games would be played with replacement players. In September, he was re-signed to be a part of the Cowboys replacement team, which was given the mock name "Rhinestone Cowboys" by the media. He ended up playing well in those 3 games as the starter at [[offensive guard|right guard]], and was kept for the rest of the season playing mainly as a backup and on [[special teams]].

In [[1988 NFL season|1988]], he suffered a thigh bruise in training camp that forced him to miss 4 regular-season contests.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1129&dat=19880803&id=Za5RAAAAIBAJ&sjid=3G0DAAAAIBAJ&pg=6745,410534 | title=Injury wave strikes Dallas linebackers | access-date=April 21, 2023}}</ref> He appeared in 12 games with 3 starts in place of an injured [[Tom Rafferty]]. In [[1989 NFL season|1989]], he appeared in 8 games with 4 starts in place of an injured Rafferty.

===New England Patriots===
On March 23, [[1990 NFL season|1990]], he was signed in [[Plan B free agency]] by the [[New England Patriots]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1914&dat=19900716&id=kA0gAAAAIBAJ&sjid=P2UFAAAAIBAJ&pg=2953,3006216 | title=Patriots | access-date=April 21, 2023}}</ref> He was cut on September 3. He was re-signed on October 26 and released after 2 games on November 6.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1914&dat=19901107&id=XIkgAAAAIBAJ&sjid=vWUFAAAAIBAJ&pg=4004,1423110 | title=Patriots Release White | access-date=April 21, 2023}}</ref> He was re-signed on November 8 and cut on after one game on November 12.<ref>{{Cite web |date=November 13, 1990 |title=Patriots release White, re-sign Douglas |url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1990/11/13/Patriots-release-White-re-sign-Douglas/1585658472400/ |access-date=April 21, 2023 |website=UPI.com}}</ref>

==Personal life==
White worked as a [[sparring|sparring partner]] for local light and middle heavyweights during his first two years in college.
